courses.title: Investing Approaches
courses.summary: Nine short lessons on the mechanics behind common investing approaches: how risk and return relate, why diversification works, what index and active funds do, what value, growth and dividend labels mean, how regular buying and rebalancing work, how fees compound, which behavioral patterns, from overconfidence to trend-following, pull investors' decisions off course, how rebalancing is carried out in practice, and how mutual fund share classes, sales loads and breakpoints work.

lessons.title: Risk and Return
lessons.summary: What a return is, what risk really means, and why the two tend to travel together.

charts.title: Two synthetic paths over 24 months
charts.caption: Both paths start at 100. The steady path rises a little every month. The volatile path swings up and down and ends higher, but an owner who had to sell in month 4 or month 9 would have taken a loss. The chart shows how variability and loss are two different things.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Both series are invented to show the mechanism.

beats.heading: What a return is
beats.text: A return is what an investment gives back to its owner over a period, measured against what was paid for it. It has two parts.

graphic.title: A return: what comes back, against what was paid

steps.title: What it gives back over a period

beats.heading: Part one: income
beats.text: Income is cash the asset pays out while it is held, such as interest on a bond or a dividend on a share.

graphic.title: Income: cash paid out while the asset is held

beats.heading: Part two: capital gain or loss
beats.text: A capital gain or loss is the change in the asset's price between purchase and sale.

graphic.title: Capital gain or loss: sale price vs price paid

beats.text: Add the two, divide by the starting amount, and you have the total return for the period, usually written as a percentage per year.

terms.definition: Income received plus any change in price, expressed as a share of the amount originally paid, over a stated period.

graphic.title: Return, as a share of the amount paid
graphic.note: Over a stated period

terms.meaning: Change in price, up or down

beats.heading: What risk really means
beats.text: Risk is the word for uncertainty about that return. It has two faces.

left.label: Variability
left.detail: the return swings period to period

beats.heading: Face one: variability
beats.text: Variability means the return swings from period to period, so the holding's value is hard to predict at any given date.

graphic.title: Variability: the return swings period to period
graphic.note: Hard to predict at any given date

beats.heading: Face two: loss
beats.text: Loss means the return can be negative, so an owner can end up with less than they started with, or with nothing.

graphic.title: Loss: ending with less than was put in

beats.text: Both faces matter. An asset can be highly variable yet rarely lose money over long stretches, or steady for years and then fail completely.

graphic.title: Both faces matter: swings vs outright failure

beats.heading: Two synthetic paths
beats.text: Both paths start at 100. The steady path rises a little every month. The volatile path swings up and down and ends higher.
But an owner who had to sell the volatile path in month 4 or month 9 would have taken a loss. Variability and loss are two different things.

terms.definition: How widely an asset's return swings from period to period; a measure of variability, not of direction.

beats.heading: A ladder of asset types
beats.text: Each step up, from cash and short-term government bills to bonds to shares, carries a higher expected return and wider swings around it.
The ladder shows a tendency observed over long periods, not a promise for any single year.

beats.heading: Why risk and return travel together
beats.text: Because buyers set prices. Nobody accepts wide swings and a real chance of loss for the same expected payoff a steady asset offers.

graphic.title: Same expected payoff, wider swings: no buyers

beats.text: So a variable asset only finds buyers at a price low enough that its expected return is higher. That gap is the risk premium.

terms.definition: The extra return, on average and over long periods, that holders of a variable asset have received compared with a steady one.

beats.text: It is a tendency across many assets and many years, not a rule for any one asset: more risk widens the range of outcomes, including the bad ones.

graphic.title: More risk widens the range of outcomes
graphic.note: A tendency across many assets and years, not a rule for one asset

check.question: How are risk and expected return linked?
choices: Riskier assets always earn more, every year
Riskier assets tend to offer higher expected returns to compensate for uncertainty
check.explanation: Buyers only accept wider swings and possible loss at a price that offers a higher expected payoff. That relationship holds on average and over time, never as a guarantee for any single asset or year.

terms.definition: The number of months, years, or decades before the money is needed; a longer horizon gives more room to wait out swings.

graphic.title: A longer horizon leaves more room to wait

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson explains how risk and return are related. It does not say how much risk anyone ought to take.
That depends on personal circumstances, goals, and time horizon, which no lesson can know.

items: Return = income + price change, against the starting amount.
Risk has two faces: variability and outright loss.
Higher expected return compensates for more uncertainty.
It is a long-run tendency, not a promise.

lessons.title: Diversification
lessons.summary: Why spreading money across many holdings smooths the ride, and which kind of risk it cannot remove.

charts.title: Yearly returns: one holding vs a basket of 20
charts.caption: Ten illustrative years. The single holding swings between a 31 percent gain and a 24 percent loss. The basket of 20 holdings moves in the same direction most years but within a much narrower band, because the company-specific surprises partly cancel. The basket still has down years: shared market risk remains.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Both series are invented to show how averaging narrows the range.

beats.heading: Spread, not concentrated
beats.text: Diversification means spreading money across many different holdings instead of concentrating it in one. To see why it works, split risk into two kinds.

graphic.title: Concentrated vs spread

terms.definition: Risk that belongs to one company or asset alone, such as a failed product, a flooded factory, a departing manager or a lawsuit.

graphic.title: Idiosyncratic risk belongs to one company

steps.title: Hits that one company or asset

terms.definition: Risk shared by nearly all assets at once, such as a recession, a jump in interest rates or a global shock.

graphic.title: Market risk is shared by nearly all assets

steps.title: Hits nearly all assets at once

beats.text: The first kind can be diluted by owning many things. The second kind cannot be diversified away.

left.label: Idiosyncratic risk
left.detail: can be diluted by owning many things

beats.heading: One basket or many
beats.text: Picture one basket holding one egg, next to many baskets each holding one egg. A shock hits one basket.
On the left the whole holding is lost. On the right a single egg is lost and the rest are untouched.
Diversification does not stop shocks. It limits how much any one shock can do.

beats.heading: The mechanism is averaging
beats.text: Company-specific shocks are largely independent: a bad year for one firm says little about the next.

graphic.title: Company-specific shocks are largely independent

beats.text: Added together, many independent ups and downs partly cancel, so the combined return swings far less than any single piece.
The more holdings, and the less alike they are, the stronger the effect.

terms.definition: How closely two assets' returns move together; the lower it is, the more their swings cancel when combined.

graphic.title: Correlation: how closely returns move together

beats.heading: What the SEC's guide notes
beats.text: A stock portion made of only four or five companies is not diversified. It takes at least a dozen carefully chosen companies to get there.

graphic.title: SEC's guide: companies in a stock portion
graphic.note: Number of carefully chosen companies in the stock portion

beats.heading: One holding vs a basket of 20
beats.text: Over ten illustrative years, the single holding swings between a 31 percent gain and a 24 percent loss.
The basket of 20 moves in the same direction most years, but within a much narrower band, because the company-specific surprises partly cancel.
The basket still has down years: shared market risk remains.
What diversification cannot do is remove market risk. If a recession pulls down almost every company, owning 500 of them instead of 5 helps little.

graphic.title: More holdings dilute specific risk, not market risk

beats.text: The shock is shared rather than specific. That is why a well-spread basket of shares still has losing years.

graphic.title: A shared shock reaches even a spread basket

steps.title: The basket still has a losing year

beats.heading: Spreading across asset categories
beats.text: Holding bonds and cash alongside shares can soften this further, because the categories have historically not moved together.

graphic.title: Categories that do not move together soften swings

beats.text: Even so, nothing removes the risk of the market as a whole. Diversification narrows the range of outcomes; it does not guarantee a gain or rule out a loss.

check.question: Someone holds 40 companies across many industries. A deep recession arrives. Most likely?
choices: It falls: recession is market risk diversification does not remove
Only one company falls, the rest untouched
check.explanation: Diversification dilutes company-specific shocks. A recession is a shared shock that pulls down most companies together, so a spread-out holding still declines, though usually less erratically than any single company.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson describes what diversification does and does not do. It is not a suggestion about how many holdings anyone needs or which ones to own.

items: Idiosyncratic risk is specific; market risk is shared.
Many unlike holdings let specific shocks partly cancel.
Market risk remains however many holdings are added.
Diversification limits damage; it guarantees no gain.

lessons.title: Index Funds vs Active Management
lessons.summary: What an index fund does, what an active manager tries to do, and what the SEC says about costs and outcomes.

charts.title: Same holdings, different costs: value of $10,000 over 30 years
charts.caption: Two synthetic funds hold identical securities that earn 6 percent a year before costs. One charges 0.2 percent a year, the other 1.0 percent. The bars show the value every five years. The gap is the cost difference compounding, not any difference in skill.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Growth rate and costs are invented to show the mechanism.

beats.heading: What a market index is
beats.text: A market index is a list of securities, such as the shares of a set of large companies, with a rule for how much weight each gets.

graphic.title: A market index: a list plus a weighting rule

steps.title: A list of securities
steps.detail: such as shares of a set of large companies

steps.title: A rule for each one's weight

beats.text: Its value tracks how the whole list performs.

terms.definition: A rule-based list of securities whose combined value is used to measure how a market or a segment of it performs.

graphic.title: An index's value tracks its list as a whole
graphic.note: Thin lines: securities on the list

beats.text: Nobody can buy an index directly. An index fund is a pooled fund that tries to match one by holding the same securities in roughly the same proportions, or a representative sample.

graphic.title: An index vs an index fund

beats.text: Because it copies a list rather than making choices, this is called a passive approach. Its return is meant to be roughly the index's return before fees.

terms.definition: A pooled fund that aims to match the return of a chosen index, before fees, by holding its securities or a sample of them.

graphic.title: An index fund's aim, in one line
graphic.note: Matches the index before fees, by holding its securities or a sample

beats.heading: Active management does the opposite
beats.text: An actively managed fund's manager chooses which securities to hold and when to trade them, pursuing a stated goal, often to do better than a benchmark index.

graphic.title: Active management: a manager makes the choices

steps.title: Pursues a stated goal
steps.detail: often to do better than a benchmark index

beats.text: That effort costs money: analysts, research, and more frequent trading.

left.label: Index fund
left.detail: copies a list, makes no choices

terms.definition: A fund manager choosing holdings and trades in an attempt to meet a goal, often to outpace a benchmark index.

graphic.title: An active fund tries to outpace a benchmark
graphic.note: An attempt: the result depends on the manager

beats.heading: The SEC's trade-off
beats.text: An active fund has the potential to do better than its benchmark, but the result depends heavily on the manager's skill, and the extra activity usually means higher fees and trading costs.

graphic.title: The SEC's trade-off for active funds

beats.heading: What the SEC's pages state
beats.text: Passive management usually means less trading, lower fees, and fewer taxable gains.

graphic.title: What passive management usually means

beats.text: If two funds hold the same securities and one charges more, the cheaper fund generally leaves more return for its owners.

graphic.title: Same holdings, different fees

steps.title: Same securities
steps.detail: so the same return before costs

beats.heading: Same holdings, different costs
beats.text: Two synthetic funds hold identical securities that earn 6 percent a year before costs. One charges 0.2 percent a year, the other 1.0 percent.
The bars show the value every five years. The gap is the cost difference compounding, not any difference in skill.

check.question: Same holdings; fees 0.3 vs 1.2 percent a year. Likely result, per the SEC?
choices: Costlier fund wins via better research
Cheaper fund generally leaves owners more return
check.explanation: With identical holdings the returns before costs are identical, so the fee gap is the whole difference. Both funds still carry the full risk of the securities they hold.

beats.text: The SEC also cautions that not every index fund is cheaper than every active fund.

graphic.title: Not every index fund costs less than every active fund

beats.text: An index fund can trail its own index because of fees, trading costs, and imperfect tracking.

terms.definition: The gap between an index fund's return and its index, caused by fees, trading costs, and sampling.

graphic.title: Tracking error: the gap between fund and index
graphic.note: From fees, trading costs and sampling

beats.heading: The arithmetic behind the debate
beats.text: Every share is owned by someone, so across all owners together the return before costs is simply the market's return.

graphic.title: All owners together earn the market return
graphic.note: Before costs: every share is owned by someone

beats.text: Index funds that hold the whole market earn roughly that return before costs. So the remaining owners, the active managers, must as a group earn it too.

graphic.title: The arithmetic, before costs

steps.title: All owners earn the market return
So active, as a group, does too

beats.text: For one active manager to do better, another must do worse. So active management as a whole roughly matches the market before costs.
After costs it trails the market, because it spends more on research and trading.
Individual managers can and do outpace their benchmarks in a given period. The arithmetic is about the average across all of them.

graphic.title: Some managers outpace; the arithmetic is the average
graphic.note: Schematic spread after costs: the average trails, some individuals lead

beats.heading: Not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson compares two approaches and reports what a public regulator states. It does not say which approach anyone ought to use; both carry the full risk of the securities they hold.

items: Index funds copy a list, before fees.
Active funds choose holdings, usually at higher cost.
As a group, active trails the market after costs.
Any fund can trail its benchmark.

lessons.title: Value, Growth and Dividends
lessons.summary: What the labels value and growth describe, what a dividend is, and how price relates to earnings.

charts.title: Illustrative price-to-earnings ranges by style label
charts.caption: Four invented style categories from left to right: high-dividend, value, broad market, and growth. For each, the two bars mark the low and high end of an illustrative P/E range. The point is the pattern, with growth labels sitting at higher multiples of earnings, not the specific numbers.
charts.xLabel: Style label (1 = high-dividend, 2 = value, 3 = broad market, 4 = growth)
charts.yLabel: Price divided by earnings per share
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Ranges are invented to show how the labels relate to the ratio.

beats.heading: Labels, not guarantees
beats.text: Value and growth are labels for styles of describing shares, not guarantees.

left.label: Value
left.detail: low price relative to earnings or assets

beats.heading: The value label
beats.text: A share labeled value trades at a low price relative to the company's earnings or assets. The buyer's idea is that the price understates what the business is worth.

graphic.title: Value: a low price relative to earnings or assets

steps.title: Low price vs earnings or assets

beats.heading: The growth label
beats.text: A share labeled growth trades at a high price relative to its earnings, because buyers anticipate that those earnings will expand quickly.

graphic.title: Growth: a high price relative to earnings

steps.title: They pay a high price vs earnings

beats.text: Both labels are judgments about a price and the profits behind it, and both can turn out wrong.

graphic.title: Both labels are judgments, and can be wrong

beats.heading: What a dividend is
beats.text: A dividend is a portion of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, usually in cash and on a regular schedule.

graphic.title: A dividend: profit paid out to shareholders

steps.title: Pays a portion to shareholders
steps.detail: usually in cash, on a regular schedule

beats.text: It is distributed profit: money the company earned and chose to hand back rather than keep.
Nothing obliges a company to pay one, and a board can cut or stop a dividend at any time.

graphic.title: A board can cut or stop a dividend at any time
graphic.note: Nothing obliges a company to pay one

beats.text: Large dividend payers are often mature, with fewer places to reinvest. Companies labeled growth often pay little or nothing, plowing profit back into the business.

terms.definition: A portion of profit paid out to shareholders, usually in cash; declared by the board and never guaranteed.
Yearly dividends per share divided by the share price, expressed as a percentage.

graphic.title: Dividend yield

beats.heading: Price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E
beats.text: The most common way to relate a price to earnings: the share price divided by earnings per share over the past twelve months.

terms.definition: A company's profit over a period divided by the number of shares outstanding; the profit attributable to one share.

beats.heading: An illustration
beats.text: A share priced at $50 with earnings of $2.50 per share has a P/E of 20. The buyer pays 20 dollars for each dollar of yearly profit.

graphic.title: $50 share price vs $2.50 earnings: a P/E of 20
graphic.note: 20 dollars paid for each dollar of yearly profit

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share; how many dollars a buyer pays for each dollar of yearly profit.

graphic.title: Price-to-earnings ratio

beats.text: A high P/E and a low P/E say different things about buyers.

left.label: High P/E
left.detail: buyers expect growth or view earnings as safe

right.label: Low P/E
right.detail: buyers expect little growth or see more risk

beats.text: The ratio compares a price with its own past or with other companies. It is not a verdict on whether the price is right.

graphic.title: P/E compares with its own past or other companies
graphic.note: A comparison, not a verdict on whether the price is right

beats.heading: P/E ranges by style label
beats.text: Four invented style categories, left to right: high-dividend, value, broad market, and growth. For each, two bars mark the low and high end of an illustrative P/E range.
The point is the pattern, with growth labels sitting at higher multiples of earnings, not the specific numbers.

check.question: Price $80; past-year earnings $4 per share. The P/E and its meaning?
choices: 20; $20 paid per dollar of yearly earnings
check.explanation: P/E is price divided by earnings per share: 80 divided by 4 equals 20. It shows how much buyers pay per dollar of profit, and says nothing alone about whether that price is right.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: Value, growth, and dividend are descriptions, not rankings. This lesson explains what the labels mean; it does not suggest one style is better, or that any ratio signals a good price.

items: Value and growth are labels, not guarantees.
A dividend can be cut or stopped anytime.
P/E = price ÷ earnings per share.
Ratios do not settle whether a price is right.

lessons.title: Dollar-Cost Averaging, Allocation and Rebalancing
lessons.summary: Buying a fixed amount at set intervals, choosing a mix of asset categories, and pulling the mix back when it drifts.

charts.title: Units bought with $100 a month at synthetic prices
charts.caption: Twelve monthly purchases of $100 each. When the price dips to $15 in month 4 the fixed sum buys 6.67 units; when it climbs to $26 in month 12 it buys 3.85. Across the year $1,200 buys 60.29 units at an average cost of $19.91 per unit, while the simple average of the twelve prices is $20.50.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Prices are invented to show the mechanism.

beats.heading: A fixed sum, on a schedule
beats.text: Dollar-cost averaging means putting the same amount of money into an investment at regular intervals, whatever the price is doing.

graphic.title: The same sum on a schedule, whatever the price
graphic.note: The same amount at each regular date

beats.text: Because the amount is fixed, each purchase buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high.
So the average cost per unit comes out below the simple average of the prices paid.

graphic.title: Average cost vs simple average price
graphic.note: More units come from low-price purchases, so cost lands below the average price

terms.meaning: All the fixed sums added up

beats.text: Anyone contributing a set sum from each paycheck into a retirement account is doing this, whether or not they call it that.

graphic.title: A set sum from each paycheck

beats.text: Twelve monthly purchases of $100 each. When the price dips to $15 in month 4 the fixed sum buys 6.67 units; when it climbs to $26 in month 12 it buys 3.85.
Across the year, $1,200 buys 60.29 units at an average cost of $19.91 per unit. The simple average of the twelve prices is $20.50.
The average cost is lower than the average price by construction, not luck: more of the money lands on the cheap purchases.
The method does not guarantee a profit or protect against a falling price. If the price ends the year below the $19.91 average cost, the holding is worth less than the $1,200 put in.

graphic.title: If the price ends below the $19.91 average cost

check.question: Why is the average cost per unit below the average price paid?
choices: A fixed sum buys more units when prices are low, fewer when high
check.explanation: A fixed dollar amount buys more units when the price is low. That pulls the average cost below the simple average of prices, but does not prevent a loss if the price ends lower still.

beats.text: Spreading purchases across time spreads the risk of buying everything at a high point, and removes the temptation to guess when to buy.

graphic.title: One purchase date vs purchases spread over time

beats.text: The trade-off runs the other way too: money held back for later purchases sits uninvested and misses any rise in the meantime.

graphic.title: Money held back misses any rise meanwhile
graphic.note: If prices rise while it waits

beats.text: So when a large sum is available all at once, spreading it out is a debated choice rather than a settled rule.

graphic.title: A large sum: a debated choice

beats.heading: Asset allocation is the mix
beats.text: What share of a holding sits in each broad category, such as shares, bonds, and cash.
The SEC describes it as a personal decision that depends mainly on time horizon and risk tolerance.
Historically, shares have had the widest swings and highest long-run returns, bonds a middle position, and cash the steadiest values and lowest returns, with inflation as the main risk.
Because the categories have not moved together, holding more than one tends to smooth the ride.
The pie's slices are labeled illustrative because no single mix suits everyone: the right proportions depend on when the money is needed and how much variability the owner can live with.
Suppose a mix starts at 60 percent shares and 40 percent bonds. After a strong run, shares might grow to 75 percent of the total without anyone buying more.

beats.heading: Rebalancing
beats.text: The mix now carries more variability than was chosen. Rebalancing brings it back: selling some of what grew and buying what shrank, or steering new contributions toward the smaller slice.

graphic.title: Shares slice: start, after the run, rebalanced
graphic.note: Sell some of what grew and buy what shrank, or steer new contributions

beats.text: It can follow a calendar, say every six or twelve months, or a band that a slice must not stray past.

graphic.title: Two ways to decide when to rebalance

beats.text: Selling can trigger transaction costs and taxes, which is part of the trade-off.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson explains three mechanisms. It does not say how much to contribute, which mix to hold, or when to rebalance; those depend on personal facts a lesson cannot know.

items: Fixed sums buy more units when prices are low.
Average cost falls below average price; losses remain possible.
Allocation depends on time horizon and risk tolerance.
Rebalancing restores the target mix, at possible cost.

lessons.title: Costs and Fees
lessons.summary: Expense ratios, sales loads, and trading costs, and how a seemingly small yearly fee compounds over decades.

charts.title: Value of $10,000 over 40 years: 0.1 percent vs 1.0 percent yearly fee
charts.caption: Both synthetic paths earn 5 percent a year before costs. After 40 years the low-fee path reaches about $67,767 and the high-fee path about $48,010. The fee gap is only 0.9 percentage points a year, yet it consumes roughly 29 percent of the ending value.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. The growth rate and fees are invented to show compounding.

beats.heading: Every pooled fund has running costs
beats.text: Paying the manager, keeping records, legal and audit work, sometimes marketing.

graphic.title: Every pooled fund has running costs

beats.heading: The expense ratio
beats.text: Funds pass these costs to their owners through the expense ratio: the percentage of the fund's assets taken each year to cover them.

graphic.title: The expense ratio passes costs to owners

steps.title: Taken from the fund each year

beats.text: An expense ratio of 1 percent means that on a $10,000 holding, $100 a year is deducted before the owner sees any return.
It is not billed separately. It comes quietly out of the fund's value, which is why it is easy to overlook. The figure appears in a standardized fee table in the prospectus.

graphic.title: Not billed: it comes out of the fund

steps.title: No separate bill, easy to overlook
Shown in the prospectus fee table

terms.definition: The share of a fund's assets deducted each year to pay its operating costs, including management and distribution fees.

graphic.title: Expense ratio
graphic.note: Deducted each year; includes management and distribution fees

beats.heading: Sales load
beats.text: A one-off charge, like a commission, paid when buying fund shares (front-end) or selling them (back-end).

beats.heading: Trading costs
beats.text: They arise whenever securities change hands: a broker's commission, or a markup when a dealer sells from its own stock.

graphic.title: Two trading costs

beats.heading: Bid-ask spread
beats.text: A third trading cost: the spread between the price at which a security can be bought and the slightly lower price at which it can be sold at the same moment.

graphic.title: Bid-ask spread: buy price vs sell price
graphic.note: At the same moment, the sell price is slightly lower

beats.heading: The SEC's fee bulletin
beats.text: Commissions, markups, and sales loads are transaction fees, charged each time an investment is bought or sold.

graphic.title: Transaction fees: charged per trade

beats.text: Ongoing fees, like the expense ratio, are charged every year the holding exists.

left.label: Transaction fees
left.detail: charged each time bought or sold

terms.definition: The cumulative reduction in a holding's value caused by fees compounding year after year.

beats.text: Picture two growth paths that start together and drift apart as a yearly fee compounds.
The gap is small in the early years and wide by the end, because each year's fee also removes the growth that money would have earned in every later year.

beats.heading: Why a 1 percent fee does damage
beats.text: Because it compounds against the owner. A fee taken in year one does not just cost that year's 1 percent.

graphic.title: Why a 1% fee costs more than 1%

steps.title: Year one: a 1% fee is taken
Its later growth is lost too

beats.text: The money removed would have grown every year afterward, so its absence is felt for decades.

beats.heading: 0.1 vs 1.0 percent yearly fee
beats.text: Both synthetic paths earn 5 percent a year before costs. After 40 years the low-fee path reaches about $67,767 and the high-fee path about $48,010.
The fee gap is only 0.9 percentage points a year, yet it consumes roughly 29 percent of the ending value.

graphic.title: A 0.9-point gap takes roughly 29% of the ending value

beats.heading: The SEC's example
beats.text: A hypothetical $100,000 grows 4 percent a year for 20 years. A 1.00 percent yearly fee leaves it tens of thousands of dollars behind the same portfolio charged 0.25 percent.

graphic.title: $100,000 at 4% for 20 years: 0.25% vs 1.00% fee
graphic.note: Computed with each fee subtracted from the 4% return every year

beats.text: Fees are one of the few facts about an investment known in advance.

graphic.title: Fees are known in advance; returns are not

check.question: Why does a 1 percent yearly fee take far more than 1 percent over 30 years?
choices: Each fee also removes that money's later growth
A penalty on the original amount
check.explanation: Fees compound. Money removed early forfeits every later year of growth, so the cumulative gap between a low-fee and a high-fee path widens over time, far exceeding the simple sum of the yearly percentages.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson explains how costs work and compound. It does not say the cheapest option is always right for anyone.
A fee is one fact among many, and every fund carries the risks of what it holds.

items: The expense ratio comes out of fund value every year.
Loads and trading costs are charged per transaction.
Yearly fees compound against the owner.
Fees are disclosed in advance, in the prospectus.

lessons.title: Behavioral Biases
lessons.summary: Overconfidence, loss aversion, the disposition effect and trend-following, and how they can turn into buying after rises and selling after falls.

charts.title: Same fund, two owners: holding vs following the trend
charts.caption: Both owners start with $10,000 in the same synthetic fund. The first holds throughout, so that line is the fund's price times 100 units: up to a peak of $13,000 in month 8, down to $9,500 in month 14, and back to $12,500 by month 24. The second sits in cash at $10,000 until the rise looks convincing, buys in month 6 at a price of 125, sells after the slide in month 13 at 100, and buys back in month 20 at 115. That owner ends month 24 with about $8,696, against $12,500 for holding. Same fund, same months: the whole gap comes from when the money went in and out.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. The prices and the buy and sell months are invented so the timing effect is easy to see.

series.name: Bought after the rise, sold after the fall (illustrative)

beats.heading: Behavioral finance
beats.text: It studies the social, mental and emotional factors that pull real decisions away from the calm, self-interested investor of textbook models.

graphic.title: The textbook investor vs real decisions

beats.text: It holds that the departures are not random: investors tend to make the same mistakes again and again.

graphic.title: The departures are not random

beats.text: The Library of Congress's Federal Research Division prepared a report for the SEC that lists common investor mistakes.

The mistakes it lists: holding too few investments, trading often, following the herd, favoring the familiar, selling winners while holding on to losers, and giving in to optimism, short-term thinking and overconfidence.

graphic.title: Mistakes the report lists

beats.text: Overconfidence is a bias of judgment. The report describes it as common among investors and a trigger for a wide range of investment errors; one place it shows up is trading activity.

graphic.title: Overconfidence: a bias of judgment

steps.title: Overconfidence
steps.detail: common among investors, per the report

steps.title: A wide range of investment errors

beats.text: In a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper issued in May 2006, Mark Grinblatt and Matti Keloharju combined investors' stock trades with data from their tax filings, driving records and psychological profiles.

graphic.title: What the working paper combined

beats.text: Investors measured as overconfident, and those most prone to sensation seeking, traded more often, even after the authors controlled for wealth, income, age, occupation and other factors.

graphic.title: More overconfidence, more trading
graphic.note: Also for sensation seekers, after controls for wealth, income and age

beats.text: The Library of Congress report links active trading with overconfidence and concludes that active trading generally leaves an investor's portfolio underperforming.

graphic.title: The report's link: trading and results

beats.heading: Loss aversion
beats.text: It comes from prospect theory, developed by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. Applied to investing, it describes people attaching more importance to avoiding losses than to achieving gains.

graphic.title: Loss aversion: avoiding losses weighs more

beats.text: Loss aversion is closely tied to the disposition effect.

terms.definition: The tendency to sell investments that have gained too soon and to hold investments that have lost for too long.

graphic.title: The disposition effect

beats.text: The report describes loss-averse investors selling strong performers in the hope of making up losses on weak ones.

right.label: Weak ones
right.detail: held, hoping to make up losses

beats.text: The SEC's bulletin on the report notes that in the months after such sales, the winners that were sold often kept outperforming the losers still held.

check.question: An investor sells a fund that gained and keeps one that lost, hoping to make up the loss. Which pattern is this?
check.explanation: The disposition effect is the tendency to sell winners too soon and hold losers too long. The report ties it to loss aversion: investors sell strong performers hoping to recoup losses on weak ones.

beats.heading: Momentum investing
beats.text: As the report defines it: buying securities with high recent returns and selling those with low recent returns, expecting the trend to continue.
The report cites researchers who tie momentum investing to herd behavior, and notes that it can give rise to speculative bubbles.

graphic.title: Momentum, herding and bubbles

steps.title: Can give rise to bubbles
steps.detail: speculative bubbles, as the report notes

beats.heading: Manias and panics
beats.text: The crowd-sized version: a rapid price rise fed by collective enthusiasm, then a sharp decline when wide-scale selling sets in.
Together these habits tend to put money in after prices have climbed and take it out after they have dropped. The next chart exaggerates that pattern on purpose.

graphic.title: Money in after a climb, out after a drop

beats.heading: Same fund, two owners
beats.text: Both owners start with $10,000 in the same synthetic fund. The first holds throughout, so that line is the fund's price times 100 units.
The held line rises to a peak of $13,000 in month 8, falls to $9,500 in month 14, and is back to $12,500 by month 24.
The second owner sits in cash at $10,000 until the rise looks convincing, then buys in month 6 at a price of 125.
That owner sells after the slide in month 13 at 100, and buys back in month 20 at 115.
The second owner ends month 24 with about $8,696. Same fund, same months: the whole gap comes from when the money went in and out.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: These are patterns researchers have found across groups of investors, not a diagnosis of any one person.
This lesson does not say when anyone ought to buy or sell. Real prices do not announce their peaks and troughs in advance.

items: Investors tend to repeat mistakes, not err at random.
Overconfident investors trade more; active trading is linked to underperformance.
Loss aversion can mean selling winners, keeping losers.
Trend-following buys after rises, sells after falls.

lessons.title: Rebalancing in Practice
lessons.summary: Calendar and tolerance-band rebalancing, steering new money instead of selling, what drift does to risk, and the costs that come with each route.

charts.title: Stock share of a 60/40 mix over 10 years
charts.caption: A synthetic mix starts at 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, and each year the two categories earn invented returns. Left alone, the stock share wanders upward and reaches 72.24 percent by year 10. The second line checks the mix once a year against a tolerance band of 55 to 65 percent. It finds the share outside the band twice, at 66.65 percent at the end of year 5 and 66.14 percent at the end of year 10, and resets it to 60 percent both times, which is why those two points sit on the target. In every other year it stays inside the band, between 57.50 and 64.35 percent.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. Yearly returns, the band and the once-a-year check are invented to show the mechanism.

series.name: Reset when outside 55–65 percent, checked yearly (illustrative)

beats.heading: Drift
beats.text: A mix's proportions change gradually as its categories earn different returns, with no buying or selling. If stocks climb faster than bonds, the stock slice grows without anyone buying more.

graphic.title: Drift: stocks climb faster, their slice grows
graphic.note: No buying or selling: uneven returns alone shift the mix

beats.text: The whole holding then takes on more of the risk that stocks carry. The SEC's beginners' guide describes stocks as having historically had the greatest risk of the three main categories.

graphic.title: Three main categories, by historical risk

beats.heading: Rebalancing
beats.text: The guide defines it as bringing a portfolio back to its original mix, so that it does not overemphasize any category and returns to a comfortable level of risk.

graphic.title: Rebalancing returns a mix to its original shares

beats.heading: Stock share of a 60/40 mix
beats.text: A synthetic mix starts at 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, and each year the two categories earn invented returns.
Left alone, the stock share wanders upward and reaches 72.24 percent by year 10.
The second line checks the mix once a year against a tolerance band of 55 to 65 percent.
It finds the share outside the band twice: at 66.65 percent at the end of year 5 and 66.14 percent at the end of year 10.
It resets the share to 60 percent both times, which is why those two points sit on the target. In every other year it stays inside the band, between 57.50 and 64.35 percent.

terms.definition: The proportions chosen for each category, such as a set share in stocks and in bonds, that rebalancing returns to.

graphic.title: A target mix: this lesson's example
graphic.note: The example used in this lesson, not a suggested mix

beats.heading: Two ways to decide when
beats.text: Calendar rebalancing checks the mix on fixed dates, such as every six or twelve months. The guide notes its advantage: the calendar itself is the reminder.

graphic.title: Two ways to decide when

terms.definition: Resetting a mix on fixed dates, such as every six or twelve months, whatever the size of the drift.

graphic.title: Calendar rebalancing
graphic.note: Whatever the size of the drift

beats.heading: Threshold rebalancing
beats.text: It sets limits in advance, a tolerance band around each target, and acts only when a slice moves outside them, so the investments themselves signal when to act.
One category's share of a mix is plotted over time. A dashed line marks the target share, and a shaded tolerance band surrounds it.
The share drifts upward until it reaches the band's top edge, where a dot marked Rebalanced shows it dropping straight back to the target. Afterward it drifts again, still inside the band.

terms.definition: A range set in advance around a target share; threshold rebalancing acts only when the share moves outside it.

graphic.title: Inside vs outside the tolerance band

check.question: Target 60 percent stocks, band 55–65 percent, check finds 63 percent. Threshold rebalancing does what?
choices: Trades, because it is above target
check.explanation: A threshold approach acts only when a share leaves its band, here below 55 or above 65 percent. At 63 percent, above target but inside the band, no trade is triggered yet.

beats.heading: Each has a blind spot
beats.text: A calendar can prompt a trade after a tiny drift, or wait while a large one builds between dates.

graphic.title: A calendar's blind spot: tiny or large drift

beats.text: A band checked only occasionally can be overshot before anyone looks. In the chart, the yearly check finds the share already at 66.65 percent at the end of year 5.

beats.heading: Rebalancing need not mean selling
beats.text: The guide describes three routes. One: sell some of an overweighted category and use the money to buy an underweighted one.

graphic.title: Route one: sell and buy

steps.title: Sell some of what is overweighted

beats.text: Two: buy more of the underweighted category. Three, for someone making regular contributions: direct them to the underweighted category until the mix is back in balance.

graphic.title: Three routes back to the target mix

beats.heading: An illustration
beats.text: Suppose $100,000 starts at 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, and in one year the stocks gain 30 percent and the bonds 2.5 percent.
The holding becomes $78,000 in stocks and $41,000 in bonds, a total of $119,000, with stocks at about 65.5 percent.

graphic.title: $78,000 of $119,000 in stocks: about 65.5%

beats.heading: Restoring it with a sale
beats.text: Selling $6,600 of stocks and buying bonds restores the mix at $71,400 and $47,600.

beats.heading: Or with new money
beats.text: Adding $11,000 of new money, all of it to bonds, also restores the mix without any sale: $78,000 is 60 percent of $130,000.

beats.heading: Each route has trade-offs
beats.text: Before rebalancing, the guide says to check whether the chosen method will trigger transaction fees or tax consequences.

graphic.title: Before rebalancing, check the costs

beats.text: Steering new money avoids a sale, but restores the mix quickly only when contributions are large relative to the drift. In the example it took $11,000; a sale moved $6,600.
Rebalancing also trims whatever has lately done well and adds to whatever has lagged, the reverse of the trend-following pull described in the previous lesson.

graphic.title: Rebalancing runs against the trend

beats.text: That is a way of holding risk near a chosen level, not a promise of a higher return: a category that has lagged can keep lagging.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson does not suggest any band, schedule or mix; those choices depend on personal circumstances, costs and taxes that a lesson cannot know.

items: Drift comes from uneven returns and shifts a mix's risk.
Calendar: fixed dates. Threshold: outside the band.
Sell, buy, or redirect contributions to restore a mix.
Fees and taxes are part of the trade-off.

lessons.title: Share Classes, Loads and Breakpoints
lessons.summary: Why one mutual fund can carry several sets of fees, how front-end loads, deferred sales charges and 12b-1 fees differ, and how breakpoints reduce a load.

charts.title: $10,000 in two synthetic classes of one fund
charts.caption: Both classes hold the same synthetic portfolio, earning 5 percent a year before class costs. Class A takes a 5 percent front-end load, so $9,500 is invested, and it then grows 4.15 percent a year after 0.85 percent in yearly costs. Class C invests the full $10,000 but grows 3.40 percent a year after 1.60 percent in yearly costs. Class C is ahead through year 7, by $9 at that point; Class A is ahead from year 8 and leads by $1,907 at year 20. The values are before any deferred sales charge, which in this example would apply only to a Class C sale in the first year.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — not real market data. The return, load and yearly costs are invented to show how a crossover arises.

beats.heading: One fund, several classes
beats.text: One mutual fund can sell several classes of shares while keeping a single portfolio and a single investment adviser.

graphic.title: One fund, several classes of shares

terms.definition: One of several types of shares in the same mutual fund, each owning the same portfolio but carrying its own fees and expenses.

graphic.title: Share classes: same portfolio, own fees

beats.text: Because each class can carry its own fees and expenses, owners of different classes of the same fund earn different returns.

graphic.title: Different fees, different returns

formula.expression: Class return = Fund return − Class costs

beats.heading: What the SEC's bulletin notes
beats.text: The effect of these fee differences compounds over time, and the class with the lowest initial fees may not be the class with the lowest fees over time.

graphic.title: Lowest fees at first may not stay lowest
graphic.note: Fee differences compound over time, per the SEC's bulletin

beats.text: Three charges do most of the sorting. The first:

terms.definition: A charge taken as a percentage of the purchase price, so that part of the money paid is not invested.

graphic.title: Front-end sales load

beats.heading: FINRA's example
beats.text: A $1,000 purchase with a 5 percent charge pays $50 up front and leaves shares worth $950.

graphic.title: FINRA's example: $1,000 with a 5% charge

terms.definition: Sometimes called a back-end load: paid only when shares are sold, it normally shrinks the longer they are held, until it disappears.

graphic.title: A deferred sales charge shrinks with time held
graphic.note: Paid only on sale; normally shrinks until it disappears

beats.text: The third is part of a fund's ongoing operating expenses.

terms.definition: An ongoing fee paid out of fund assets to cover the costs of marketing and selling fund shares.

graphic.title: The 12b-1 fee: ongoing, from fund assets

beats.text: Class A shares typically carry the front-end load and a lower yearly charge. FINRA's figures for the asset-based sales charge:
Class C shares have no front-end load, so the full purchase is invested. But they often charge about 1 percent if sold within a short time, usually one year.

graphic.title: Class C: no front-end load

steps.title: Often about 1% if sold early
steps.detail: within a short time, usually one year

beats.text: Class C shares typically keep their higher yearly expenses for as long as the shares are held, instead of converting to Class A.

graphic.title: Class C keeps its higher yearly expenses
graphic.note: For as long as shares are held, instead of converting to Class A

beats.text: No-load classes skip sales loads but, like every class, still have ongoing operating costs.

graphic.title: No-load classes still have running costs

beats.heading: $10,000 in two synthetic classes
beats.text: Both classes hold the same synthetic portfolio, earning 5 percent a year before class costs.
Class A takes a 5 percent front-end load, so $9,500 is invested. It then grows 4.15 percent a year after 0.85 percent in yearly costs.
Class C invests the full $10,000 but grows 3.40 percent a year after 1.60 percent in yearly costs.
Class C is ahead through year 7, by $9 at that point. Class A is ahead from year 8 and leads by $1,907 at year 20.
The values are before any deferred sales charge, which in this example would apply only to a Class C sale in the first year.

beats.heading: The SEC's point in numbers
beats.text: Because Class C generally has a higher 12b-1 fee, the SEC's bulletin warns that an owner could end up paying more by holding it for a long time.
FINRA: Class C may cost less than Class A over a shorter horizon, since little or no sales charge is paid.
In a model like this one, where the lines cross depends on the size of the load, the gap in yearly costs and the return.

check.question: Why does C lead early, then trail?
choices: C invests more at first; higher yearly costs compound
A's load is refunded after seven years
C converts to A after year 7
check.explanation: Same portfolio. Class C invests the whole $10,000, so it leads at first; its yearly costs are 0.75 percentage point higher, and that gap compounds until Class A pulls ahead after year 7.

beats.heading: Breakpoints
beats.text: Volume discounts on the front-end load of Class A shares. The discount depends on the amount invested in a particular family of funds.

graphic.title: Breakpoints: a lower load for larger amounts
graphic.note: Depends on the amount invested in a family of funds

beats.heading: FINRA's example
beats.text: A load of 5.75 percent on purchases under $50,000, cut to 4.50 percent for $50,000 to $99,999, and reduced further or eliminated for larger amounts.

graphic.title: FINRA's example breakpoint schedule
graphic.note: Reduced further or eliminated for larger amounts

beats.text: At those rates a $49,000 purchase pays $2,817.50 in sales charges, while a $50,000 purchase pays $2,250.

graphic.title: Sales charges: $49,000 vs $50,000 purchase
graphic.note: The larger purchase pays less at those rates

beats.text: A breakpoint does not require one large purchase.

terms.definition: A commitment to buy a specified amount over a period, usually 13 months, that earns the breakpoint discount on each purchase.

graphic.title: Letter of intent

beats.heading: Rights of accumulation
beats.text: They count shares already held, and those of certain related parties such as a spouse or children, toward the threshold.

graphic.title: Rights of accumulation
graphic.note: All counted toward the breakpoint threshold

terms.meaning: Shares of a spouse or children

beats.heading: Not always applied
beats.text: FINRA's breakpoints page recounts that routine NASD examinations in 2002 found mutual fund transactions in which eligible customers did not always receive breakpoint discounts they were entitled to.

beats.heading: Education, not a recommendation
beats.text: This lesson explains how share-class costs are built and compared. It does not say which class, fund or purchase size suits anyone.
A fund's actual charges for each class are set out in its prospectus.

items: Classes share a portfolio but can charge different fees.
Front-end at purchase; deferred on sale; 12b-1 ongoing.
Which class costs less depends on holding time.
Breakpoints cut the front-end load at set levels.

courses.title: Reading Price Charts
courses.summary: Nine lessons on reading candlesticks, trends, support and resistance, candle patterns, moving averages, volume, and trend lines as a vocabulary for describing past prices - plus base rates, hindsight, and costs, and why the evidence that charts forecast prices is mixed and hard to use.

lessons.title: Candlestick Anatomy and Timeframes
lessons.summary: What one candle records, how to tell an up candle from a down candle, and why a daily and a weekly chart of the same asset look different.

charts.title: Twelve synthetic daily candles
charts.caption: Each candle is one trading day. Up candles close above their open; down candles close below it. The wicks mark the day's extremes.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: A price chart is a record of past trades. The most common style is the candlestick chart.

graphic.title: A candlestick chart: one candle per period

beats.heading: Four numbers per candle
beats.text: Each candle summarizes one slice of time, such as a minute, a day, or a week, with four numbers.
The close is the last trade of the period.

terms.definition: The price of the first trade in the period the candle covers.

beats.text: The high is the most anyone paid during the period, and the low is the least. The four numbers are often shortened to OHLC.

graphic.title: One candle records four prices

beats.text: The thick body runs from the open to the close. Thin lines above and below, called wicks or shadows, reach up to the high and down to the low.

terms.definition: The thin line above or below the body showing how far price traveled beyond the open and close.

beats.text: The body shows where the period started and finished. Close above the open: an up candle. Close below the open: a down candle.

graphic.title: An up candle and a down candle

beats.text: Color conventions vary between charting tools. In this app's charts, up candles are blue and down candles are amber.
Each candle here is one trading day. The wicks mark the day's extremes: how far trading strayed from the body before coming back.

beats.heading: Long wicks
beats.text: A long wick means the price visited that level but did not stay there.

graphic.title: A long upper wick: price visited but did not stay

check.question: A daily candle: open 100.4, high 100.9, low 99.2, close 99.6. Which is correct?
check.explanation: Up or down is decided only by comparing the close with the open. Here 99.6 is below 100.4, so the body is a down body. The high and low only set the wicks.

beats.heading: Which close counts?
beats.text: Even the close needs a definition. The SEC notes that for many U.S. markets the regular session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
After-hours trades are tagged separately, so they do not change the regular-session close, high, or low.

graphic.title: After-hours trades are kept apart

terms.definition: The price of the last trade in the period the candle covers, under whatever session rules the data provider uses.

graphic.title: How a close is chosen

beats.text: Two data vendors can still print different closes for the same day if one includes after-hours trades. A chart is only as clear as the rules behind it.

graphic.title: Two vendors, two closes for one day

beats.text: Timeframe is the length of time each candle covers.

terms.definition: The span of time one candle represents, such as one minute, one day, or one week.

graphic.title: Timeframe: the span one candle covers

beats.text: A weekly candle is not a new set of facts. It is that week's daily candles, usually five, squeezed into one.
Its open is the first trading day's open, and its close is the last trading day's close. Its high and low are the highest high and lowest low of the whole week.

graphic.title: Five daily candles and the weekly candle they make

beats.text: That is why a choppy week of daily candles can become a single calm-looking weekly candle.

check.question: Where does a weekly candle's high come from?
choices: The highest high of the whole week
check.explanation: A weekly candle's high and low are the highest high and lowest low of the whole week. Its open and close come from the first and last trading days.

items: A candle packs one period into OHLC.
Body: close versus open. Wicks: the extremes.
Longer timeframes summarize, so detail is lost.
Session rules decide the close, so charts can differ.

lessons.title: Trends and Ranges
lessons.summary: How chart readers describe rising, falling, and sideways price action, and why the label depends on the timeframe you choose.

charts.title: A synthetic uptrend that turns into a range
charts.caption: Days 1 to 14 print higher highs and higher lows. From day 15 the highs stall near 102.6 and the lows hold near 100.5, so the chart reads as a range.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: Chart readers use three words to describe the shape of past prices: uptrend, downtrend, and range.

graphic.title: Three labels for past price shapes

terms.definition: A local peak on the chart with lower prices on both sides of it.

graphic.title: A swing high: lower prices on both sides

beats.heading: Uptrend
beats.text: A stretch where each swing high is above the last swing high and each swing low is above the last swing low: higher highs and higher lows.

graphic.title: An uptrend: higher highs and higher lows

beats.text: Drawn as a channel, an uptrend has a line under the higher lows and a parallel line over the higher highs. The price zigzags between them while the whole channel slopes up.

beats.heading: Downtrend
beats.text: The mirror image of an uptrend: lower highs and lower lows.

graphic.title: A downtrend: lower highs and lower lows

beats.heading: Range
beats.text: Also called a sideways market or consolidation. The swing highs and swing lows stay at roughly the same levels, so the price moves back and forth inside a band.

graphic.title: A range: swings stay inside a band

check.question: A series prints swing highs at 98, 101, 104 and swing lows at 95, 97, 100. Which label fits that stretch of chart?
check.explanation: Each swing high (98, 101, 104) is above the previous one and each swing low (95, 97, 100) is also above the previous one. Higher highs plus higher lows is the definition of an uptrend.

beats.heading: Hindsight labels
beats.text: A trend is a description of what already happened, not a rule about what comes next.
A trend is defined by past swing points, and the label only becomes clear after the price has made them.
A run of higher highs can end at any time, and an uptrend usually looks obvious only when you are looking backward.

graphic.title: A run of higher highs, then a lower high

beats.text: This synthetic series rises for fourteen days and then drifts sideways for twelve more. Days 1 to 14 print higher highs and higher lows.
From day 15 the highs stall near 102.6 and the lows hold near 100.5, so the chart reads as a range.

beats.heading: Same data, three answers
beats.text: Imagine an asset that fell for six months, rose for three years, and drifted sideways for the past two months.

graphic.title: Fell, rose for three years, then drifted sideways

beats.text: On a five-year weekly chart it is an uptrend. On a two-month daily chart it is a range.
On a week of hourly candles it might read as a downtrend if the last few days slipped. None of those readers is wrong.

graphic.title: Same asset, three timeframes, three labels

beats.text: Each timeframe throws away different detail, so each produces a different summary of the same trades.

graphic.title: Each timeframe keeps different detail

check.question: In that example, which label does the two-month daily chart give?
check.explanation: The asset drifted sideways for the past two months, so a two-month daily chart reads as a range. The five-year weekly chart reads as an uptrend.

beats.text: This is why people who talk about a trend usually say which timeframe they mean.

graphic.title: Name the timeframe with the trend

beats.text: The SEC describes the stock market as the organized trading of stocks through exchanges, over-the-counter, and computerized trading venues.
The chart is simply a drawing of the trades that flowed through those venues. The trades are the facts.
The trend label is an interpretation laid on top, and it changes with the lens.

items: Uptrend, downtrend, and range describe past swing points.
A trend label is clear only in hindsight and can end anytime.
Change the timeframe and the label can change.
Ask which timeframe a trend claim means.

lessons.title: Support and Resistance
lessons.summary: Levels where a price has turned before, why chart readers watch them, and why they describe the past rather than promise the future.

charts.title: A synthetic price bouncing inside a band
charts.caption: Rallies stall near 104 and declines stall near 96. Each touch is marked. The bands are drawn after the fact from the turns that already happened.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: A falling price has stopped and turned up there more than once.

terms.definition: A price level at which declines have repeatedly stopped and reversed upward.

graphic.title: Support: declines that stopped near 96

beats.text: A rising price has stopped and turned down there more than once.

terms.definition: A price level at which rallies have repeatedly stopped and reversed downward.

graphic.title: Resistance: rallies that stopped near 104

beats.text: Picture a price path bouncing between two horizontal bands. The lower band is support, where declines have stopped; the upper band is resistance, where rallies have stopped.
Chart readers draw horizontal lines at these levels and watch how the price behaves near them.
The idea is simple: a level that mattered to buyers and sellers in the past may be a place where they show up again.

graphic.title: Why a past turning level gets watched

steps.title: Price turned at this level before
Orders may show up there again

beats.heading: Why would a level repeat?
beats.text: A market is a meeting place for orders. The SEC describes a market order as an instruction to buy or sell at the going price.
Many participants also leave standing orders at specific prices.

graphic.title: Two kinds of order

beats.text: If enough orders cluster near one price, they can absorb the pressure that pushed the price there, and the price turns.
Round numbers attract orders because people think in round numbers.

terms.definition: A price such as 50 or 100 that people naturally anchor on when placing orders.

graphic.title: Rallies that stalled at a round number

beats.text: A previous high attracts orders because it is a level many people remember.

graphic.title: A later rally nearing a previous high

beats.text: In this synthetic chart, rallies stall near 104 and declines stall near 96. Each touch is marked.
The bands are drawn after the fact, from the turns that already happened.

beats.heading: Descriptive, not predictive
beats.text: A support line is a summary of past turns. It says the price turned here before; it does not say the price must turn here again.
Prices break through support and resistance all the time, and when they do, chart readers simply redraw the lines.

graphic.title: Support gave way, so the line was redrawn

terms.definition: A move through a support or resistance level that had previously held.

graphic.title: A breakout: a close through a level that had held

beats.text: Treat these lines as a way to organize what you see, not as a barrier that the market has agreed to respect.

graphic.title: A line organizes the chart; it binds nothing

beats.text: A useful habit is to count the touches. A line drawn through one turn is a guess; a line touched three or four times describes something the market actually did.
Even so, more touches only improve the description of the past. Nothing in a support line says whether the next visit ends in a bounce or a break.

graphic.title: More touches describe the past better

beats.text: People drawing the same chart often place the lines a little differently.

graphic.title: Same peaks, two reasonable resistance lines

check.question: A price turned down at about 104 four times. The fifth approach?
choices: 104 was resistance; the outcome is unknown
Meaningless: four touches are too few
check.explanation: Support and resistance describe where the price has turned before. Four past turns make 104 a well-described resistance level, but past turns do not determine the next one.

items: Support and resistance mark past repeated turns.
Orders cluster at remembered prices and round numbers.
More touches improve the description, not the prediction.
Levels break often; then the lines get redrawn.

lessons.title: Common Candle Patterns and the Evidence
lessons.summary: What a doji, a hammer, and an engulfing candle each describe, and an honest look at what academic research has found about chart patterns.

charts.title: A synthetic hammer and a bullish engulfing pair
charts.caption: Day 6 is a hammer: a tiny body at the top of a long lower wick after five down days. Days 12 and 13 form a bullish engulfing pair: the up body on day 13 covers the whole down body of day 12.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: Three common candle shapes show how the vocabulary works: the doji, the hammer, and the engulfing pattern.

graphic.title: Three candle shapes and what they record

beats.text: The wicks do the talking. A doji describes a period that ended where it began.

terms.definition: A candle whose open and close are nearly equal, leaving almost no body.

graphic.title: A doji: open and close nearly equal

terms.definition: A candle seen after a decline, with a small body near its high, a lower wick at least about twice the body's length, and little or no upper wick.

graphic.title: A hammer after a decline

beats.text: A hammer describes a period in which the price fell hard, then recovered most of the drop before the close.
In this synthetic chart, day 6 is a hammer: a tiny body at the top of a long lower wick after five down days.

terms.definition: A two-candle shape in which the second body completely covers the first.

graphic.title: An engulfing pair: the second body covers the first

beats.heading: Bullish engulfing
beats.text: A small down candle is followed by a larger up candle whose body completely covers the previous body: the second period's buying more than undid the first period's selling.
Days 12 and 13 form a bullish engulfing pair: the up body on day 13 covers the whole down body of day 12. A bearish engulfing pattern is the reverse.
Each name is a compact way of saying what the open, high, low, and close did.

graphic.title: A pattern name is shorthand for OHLC

steps.title: A short name for that shape

check.question: Which candle has an open and close that are nearly equal?
check.explanation: A doji's open and close are nearly equal, leaving almost no body. A hammer has a small body near its high, and an engulfing pattern uses two candles.

terms.definition: The practice of studying past prices and volume, often through charts, to describe market behavior.

graphic.title: Technical analysis in three steps

beats.text: Researchers have tested whether chart shapes say anything about what happens next.
One test: a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper issued in March 2000 by Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky, and Jiang Wang.
They used a computer method to detect classic multi-day chart patterns, such as head-and-shoulders and double bottoms, in U.S. stock prices from 1962 to 1996.

graphic.title: The Lo, Mamaysky and Wang test: data and paper

beats.text: They asked whether the days after a pattern differed statistically from ordinary days. They reported that several patterns carried some incremental information and may have some practical value.

graphic.title: What the test asked and reported

beats.heading: Limits of the test
beats.text: Their test did not cover single-candle shapes such as the hammer, and it measured statistical differences, not profits after trading costs.

check.question: What does the Lo, Mamaysky, and Wang finding show?
choices: Trading patterns reliably profits after costs
Days after patterns differed statistically from ordinary days in their sample
check.explanation: The paper reports incremental statistical information in historical U.S. data. It does not show that acting on the patterns earns a profit once trading costs are paid, and it covers one sample period.

beats.heading: Information is not profit
beats.text: A pattern can shift the odds a little and still be useless in practice, because acting on it costs money.

graphic.title: Information is not profit

steps.title: A pattern shifts odds a little
It can be useless in practice

beats.text: Those costs include commissions, the spread between buying and selling prices, and taxes.
The wider evidence cuts both ways. Research on simple trading rules in currency markets found some predictive value.
But one study found that value shrank sharply once periods of central bank intervention were set aside.

graphic.title: Currency trading rules, with and without intervention

beats.text: A study of many stock-return patterns found that few high-turnover strategies stayed statistically significant after trading costs.

graphic.title: Anomalies after trading costs

beats.text: That makes patterns fine for reading a chart and a weak reason to act.

items: Doji, hammer, engulfing: names for OHLC shapes.
Some patterns carry information; evidence is mixed, effects can fade.
Information is not profit after costs.
Learn the vocabulary to read charts, not to trade.

lessons.title: Moving Averages and Volume
lessons.summary: How a moving average smooths a price series and why it lags, plus what trading volume measures and what it cannot tell you.

charts.title: A synthetic price and its five-day moving average
charts.caption: The average is smoother than the price but arrives late: it keeps falling for a few days after the price turns up, and keeps rising after the price turns down.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

charts.title: Synthetic daily volume for the same 24 days
charts.caption: Bars show how many units traded each day. Busy days and quiet days both occur on up days and on down days.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: Raw prices jump around. A moving average is a way to smooth them.

beats.heading: Five-day simple moving average
beats.text: It takes the last five closing prices, adds them up, and divides by five.
Each day it drops the oldest close and adds the newest, so the average moves with the price.

terms.definition: The arithmetic mean of the last N closing prices, recalculated as each new close arrives.

graphic.title: A simple moving average

formula.expression: SMA = (sum of last N closes) ÷ N

beats.text: Longer windows, such as 50 or 200 days, produce smoother lines; shorter windows hug the price more closely.

check.question: The last five closes are 100, 101, 102, 103, and 104. A new close of 99 arrives. What is the new five-day simple moving average?
check.explanation: Drop the oldest close (100), add 99: 101 + 102 + 103 + 104 + 99 = 509, and 509 ÷ 5 = 101.8. The average barely moved though the price fell 5 points.

beats.heading: Lag
beats.text: Smoothing has a price of its own. Because the average includes old closes, it can only respond to a turn after several new closes have pulled it along.
In this synthetic chart, the price bottoms on day 16, but the average keeps falling until day 18.
The average is smoother than the price but arrives late: it keeps falling for a few days after the price turns up, and keeps rising after it turns down.
The longer the window, the later the turn shows up.

terms.definition: The delay between a change in price and the moment a smoothed indicator reflects it.

graphic.title: Longer windows turn later

beats.text: A moving average therefore describes where the price has been on average, and any signal it gives is by construction behind the price.

graphic.title: Price and its average are not in step

beats.heading: Crossovers are just arithmetic
beats.text: Chart readers often talk about the price crossing above or below its moving average, or a short average crossing a long one.

terms.definition: The moment a price line passes through its moving average, or one average passes through another.

graphic.title: A crossover: price passes through its average

beats.text: Each crossing is a mechanical result of recent closes being higher or lower than the older closes inside the window: a description of the last few periods relative to the ones before.

graphic.title: Why a crossover happens

beats.text: Whether a crossing has any bearing on future prices is a separate, empirical question, and the evidence in the previous lesson applies here too.

graphic.title: Arithmetic versus an open question

beats.text: It is usually drawn as bars under the price.

terms.definition: The quantity of shares or contracts traded during a period, a measure of activity rather than direction.

beats.text: Volume measures activity, not direction: a heavy-volume day can close up or down.
In this chart of the same 24 days, bars show how many units traded each day. Busy days and quiet days both occur on up days and on down days.

check.question: What does volume measure?
choices: Direction: which way the price moved
check.explanation: Volume is the quantity of shares or contracts traded in a period. It measures activity, not direction: a heavy-volume day can close up or down.

beats.text: The SEC's note on closing prices points out that a single low-volume after-hours trade can print a price far from the 4:00 p.m. close.
That is one reason readers check volume before trusting an unusual price.

graphic.title: Before trusting an unusual price

items: A moving average is the mean of the last N closes.
Smoothing creates lag; longer windows lag more.
Volume counts how much traded, not which way.
Crossovers are arithmetic about recent closes, not forecasts.
