lessons.title: Patterns Are Not Predictions
lessons.summary: Hindsight, data-mining, survivorship, and costs: why patterns that look obvious on a chart are so hard to use, and why this course teaches reading rather than trading.

charts.title: Two synthetic random walks
charts.caption: Both series were produced by coin flips with no memory. Any trend, channel, or support level you see in them was created by chance and drawn by your eye.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic random walks generated by coin flips — not real market data.

beats.text: Human eyes are built to find shapes.

graphic.title: The eye draws a trend through wiggles

beats.text: The two series in this chart were generated by coin flips: start at 100 and each day add or subtract a random amount.
Nothing about tomorrow's move depends on what came before, yet both lines seem to show trends, support levels, and turning points.
Both series have no memory. Any trend, channel, or support level you see in them was created by chance and drawn by your eye.

terms.definition: A series whose next change does not depend on its previous changes, so its past path carries no information about its future path.

graphic.title: A random walk, step by step

check.question: Two coin-flip series seem to show trends. What made those trends?
check.explanation: Both series were produced by coin flips with no memory. Any trend, channel, or support level in them was created by chance and drawn by the eye.

beats.heading: Four traps: hindsight
beats.text: Patterns are easy to name after the outcome is known.

terms.definition: The tendency to see past events as having been predictable once their outcome is known.

graphic.title: Hindsight bias

beats.heading: Data-mining
beats.text: Test enough rules on enough history and some will look brilliant by luck.

graphic.title: How data-mining finds lucky rules

steps.title: Test many rules on one history

terms.definition: Searching many rules or variables until one fits the past by chance, then mistaking the fit for a real relationship.

graphic.title: A chance fit looks like a real one

beats.heading: Survivorship
beats.text: You hear about strategies that survived; failures drop out of the sample.

graphic.title: Survivorship: failures drop out

terms.definition: Drawing conclusions from the examples that survived while ignoring those that failed and dropped out of view.

graphic.title: Survivorship bias

beats.heading: Costs
beats.text: Every trade pays a spread, often a commission, and sometimes tax, so a rule must be right by a wide margin to break even.

graphic.title: Costs come out of every trade

steps.title: Must cover costs to break even

check.question: A rule's twenty-year past record is strong. Why be cautious?
choices: Maybe a chance fit among many rules, ignoring trading costs
check.explanation: Data-mining, hindsight, survivorship, and transaction costs make a strong historical record easy to produce and hard to repeat. A back-tested record describes the past sample; it is not evidence about the future.

beats.heading: The efficient-markets idea in plain words
beats.text: If a pattern in past prices reliably pointed to future prices, traders would act on it.
Their trading would move the price until the pattern stopped working.
On this view, whatever a public chart shows is already in the price by the time you look.

graphic.title: Why a public pattern is already priced

beats.text: Economists contest the idea at the edges, yet it explains why easy, visible patterns rarely stay useful for long.

graphic.title: The efficient-markets idea, in dispute

beats.heading: Day trading
beats.text: Rapid buying and selling within one day to catch short moves.

graphic.title: Day trading: bought and sold within one day

beats.text: The SEC's investor education site describes day trading as extremely risky and able to produce large losses very quickly.
FINRA adds that frequent intraday trading, especially on borrowed money, can end in losing some or all of what was put in.

graphic.title: Frequent intraday trading, per FINRA

steps.title: Can lose some or all put in

beats.text: The SEC also warns of pump-and-dump schemes, where fraudsters spread false or misleading hype to lift a price, then sell their own shares.
A chart never tells you why the price moved.

graphic.title: What a chart shows and leaves out

beats.heading: Why this course teaches reading, not trading
beats.text: These lessons give you vocabulary for following market reporting, not an edge over participants who know the same vocabulary and have faster tools.

graphic.title: A reading vocabulary, not an edge

beats.text: Risk, in the SEC's definition, is uncertainty about returns and the harm when they disappoint; reading a chart does not remove it.

graphic.title: Risk remains after reading a chart

steps.title: Reading a chart does not remove it

items: The eye supplies patterns in random series.
Hindsight, data-mining, survivorship, costs: four traps.
Trading on a reliable visible pattern tends to erase it.
Charts show what happened, never why.
A reading vocabulary, not an edge.

lessons.title: Volume and Confirmation
lessons.summary: What chart readers mean when they say volume confirmed a breakout, how relative volume is calculated, and what research on trading volume does and does not show.

charts.title: A thin-volume break and a heavy-volume break
charts.caption: Days 1 to 10 never trade above 105. Day 11 closes at 105.3 on 0.9 million units, about 0.6 times the average of its previous 10 days, and day 12 closes back below 105 at 104.3. Day 18 closes at 106.1 on 3.0 million units, about 2.2 times the average of its previous 10 days. The chart ends on day 18, so it shows the label, not what followed.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

charts.title: Synthetic daily volume for the same 18 days
charts.caption: Volume for the same 18 days. The bar on day 11 is the shortest in the chart and the bar on day 18 is the tallest. Each bar shows how much traded that day, not which way the price moved.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: Lesson 5 defined volume as the amount traded in a period. Chart readers put that number to one particular use: judging a breakout.

graphic.title: One use of volume

beats.heading: Breakout
beats.text: A move through a support or resistance level that had held before.

beats.heading: Confirmed
beats.text: When the price closes through a level on much heavier trading than usual, chart readers call the move confirmed.

beats.heading: Unconfirmed
beats.text: When it pushes through on unusually light trading, they call it unconfirmed, or say it came on thin volume.
Their reasoning is that heavy trading reflects broader agreement than a handful of trades.

terms.definition: Chart readers' label for a breakout that happens on heavier-than-usual volume.

graphic.title: How readers apply the confirmed label

beats.text: Usual is measured with relative volume.

terms.definition: A period's volume divided by the average volume of a chosen number of earlier periods.

beats.text: In this lesson the comparison window is the previous 10 trading days.
A relative volume of 2.0 means the day traded twice its recent average; 0.6 means it traded 60 percent of it.

graphic.title: Relative volume of 2.0 and 0.6

beats.text: The window is a choice. A 20-day or 50-day window gives a different average, and so a different ratio for the same day.

graphic.title: The window is a choice

beats.text: In this synthetic chart, days 1 to 10 never trade above 105. Day 11 closes at 105.3 on 0.9 million units, about 0.6 times its previous 10-day average.
Day 12 closes back below 105, at 104.3. Day 18 closes at 106.1 on 3.0 million units, about 2.2 times the average of its previous 10 days.

graphic.title: Volume on the two break days, millions of units

beats.text: The chart ends on day 18, so it shows the label, not what followed.
Volume for the same 18 days: day 11's bar is the shortest, day 18's the tallest. Each bar shows how much traded that day, not which way the price moved.

terms.definition: Trading that is well below a period's recent average, so relatively few units changed hands.

beats.heading: Activity, not direction
beats.text: Every unit bought on a given day was also sold by someone, so volume by itself cannot say which side was more eager.

graphic.title: Every unit bought was also sold

beats.text: A confirmation rule is still built entirely from past prices and past volume. It sorts breakouts into labeled groups after the fact.

graphic.title: A confirmation rule sorts after the fact

beats.text: It does not tell you which ones hold. A thin break can hold, and a heavy break can fail.

check.question: Prior 10-day average: 1.5 million. Breakout day: 3.3 million. Which statement is correct?
choices: 2.2: alone, it doesn't settle what's next
check.explanation: 3.3 ÷ 1.5 = 2.2. Chart readers would call that a heavy-volume break, but the ratio only describes one day's activity; it does not settle whether the price stays above the level.

beats.heading: What research shows
beats.text: Research on volume does not reduce to a simple confirmation rule.
In a 1992 NBER working paper, John Campbell, Sanford Grossman, and Jiang Wang found that the day-to-day correlation of stock index returns tends to decline as trading volume rises.
Their model explains this with traders who absorb buying or selling pressure from others who are not trading on information, and who are rewarded through changing expected returns.

graphic.title: The Campbell, Grossman and Wang model

beats.text: The model implies that a price drop on a heavy-volume day is more often linked to a rise in expected return than a drop on a light-volume day.

graphic.title: In their model: two kinds of price drop

beats.text: A 2001 NBER working paper by Guillermo Llorente, Roni Michaely, Gideon Saar, and Jiang Wang argued that price moves driven by risk-sharing trades tend to reverse.
Moves driven by trades on private information tend to continue, they argued.
They reported evidence consistent with that in daily data on individual stocks listed on two U.S. exchanges.

graphic.title: Llorente, Michaely, Saar and Wang

beats.text: Both kinds of trading add to volume, and a chart does not show which kind was behind a given day.

graphic.title: What a volume bar cannot split

beats.heading: Thin volume and liquidity
beats.text: Investor.gov describes a stock's liquidity as how rapidly its shares can be bought or sold without substantially moving the price.
Investor.gov notes that stocks with low liquidity may be difficult to sell.

terms.definition: How easily and quickly shares can be bought or sold without substantially moving the price.

graphic.title: Liquidity

beats.text: Thin volume on one day, like day 11 in the chart, is a narrower idea: fewer units than usual changed hands that day.

items: Heavy volume on a breakout: confirmed. Thin volume: doubted.
Relative volume depends on the window chosen.
A thin break can hold; a heavy break can fail.
Research links volume to returns in several ways.

lessons.title: Drawing Trend Lines
lessons.summary: How a trend line is drawn through past lows or highs, why the choice of anchor points and of closes versus intraday lows changes when a break appears, and what a false break is.

charts.title: One set of prices, two trend lines
charts.caption: Swing lows on days 3, 9 and 15 are marked. A line through the day 3 and day 9 lows rises 0.3 per day; a line through the day 3 and day 15 lows rises 0.2 per day. Lows fall below the steeper line on days 15, 16, 20, 21 and 22, and closes fall below it on days 15, 21 and 22. No low from day 3 to day 22 is below the shallower line.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed numbers, not real market data.

beats.text: Lesson 2 described an uptrend as a run of higher highs and higher lows. A trend line turns that description into a drawing.

graphic.title: Higher lows joined by a trend line

beats.text: In an uptrend, the line starts at one swing low, passes through a later and higher swing low, and is extended to the right. In a downtrend, it runs through falling swing highs instead.

terms.definition: A straight line drawn through two or more swing lows in an uptrend, or swing highs in a downtrend, and extended to the right.

graphic.title: In a downtrend the line runs over falling highs

beats.text: Two points define a line; a third touch, as with the support lines in lesson 3, only tightens the description of the past.

graphic.title: Two lows define the line; a third touch fits it

beats.text: The extended part of the line is only the past slope carried forward; it is not a forecast.

graphic.title: Past the last price, the line is only extended slope

beats.text: Any two lows define a line.

terms.definition: One of the past swing lows or highs a trend line passes through; changing it changes the slope.

graphic.title: Change one anchor and the slope changes

beats.text: In the diagram, a rising zigzag path has three marked lows, labeled 1, 2 and 3. Dashed Line A runs through lows 1 and 2 and is steeper.
Dashed Line B runs through lows 1 and 3 and is shallower. A steeper line runs closer to the latest prices, so the price tends to cross it sooner.
Near the right edge the price dips below Line A but not below Line B, which it touches at low 3: a break of one line, not the other.
A reader who drew Line A sees a break, while a reader who drew Line B sees an intact uptrend, using exactly the same prices.
In this synthetic chart, swing lows on days 3, 9 and 15 are marked.
A line through the day 3 and day 9 lows rises 0.3 per day; a line through the day 3 and day 15 lows rises 0.2 per day.

graphic.title: Two lines from the day 3 low: 0.3 and 0.2 per day

beats.text: Lows fall below the steeper line on days 15, 16, 20, 21 and 22, and closes fall below it on days 15, 21 and 22.
No low from day 3 to day 22 is below the shallower line.
A second choice is what counts as crossing. Some readers count any trade below the line, so an intraday low is enough. Others require a close below it.

graphic.title: Low below the line, close above it

beats.text: Day 20 trades as low as 101.7, below the steeper line at 102.1, but closes at 102.2, above it.
That is a break by the intraday rule and not by the closing rule. Day 15 closed below that line, yet the closes on days 16 through 20 were all back above it.

terms.definition: A move through a trend line or level that is reversed soon after, which can only be labeled in hindsight.

graphic.title: A close below a level, reversed soon after

beats.text: Whether a break was false is only known later, and the verdict depends on which line and which rule were chosen.

graphic.title: Which break counts depends on the rule

check.question: Trend line: 50 on day 1, 54 on day 5. Day 10 low 58.4, close 59.3. Which fits?
check.explanation: The line rises 1 per day, so day 10 is at 50 + 9 = 59. The 58.4 low is below it; the 59.3 close is above. Only the intraday rule counts it.

beats.heading: Short dips and stop orders
beats.text: Investor.gov explains that a stop order becomes a market order once the price reaches a chosen stop price.
A short-term fluctuation can set it off, and in a fast-moving market the trade may be filled at a different price.
So an order parked just under a trend line can be triggered by a dip that reverses before the close.
As lesson 1 noted, Investor.gov gives the regular-session close for stocks as the 4:00 p.m. price.

beats.heading: The eye is not a rule
beats.text: Because drawing lines takes judgment, researchers who test chart shapes have to replace the eye with fixed procedures.

graphic.title: The eye versus a fixed procedure

beats.text: In their 2000 NBER working paper, Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky, and Jiang Wang wrote that technical analysis is highly subjective, since the shapes people see in price charts often depend on who is looking.
They proposed a systematic, automatic method for recognizing patterns.
Scale is another hidden choice.

terms.definition: A price axis on which equal percentage changes take up equal vertical distance.

graphic.title: Ordinary and logarithmic price axes

beats.text: A straight line drawn through the same two lows on a log axis is a different line from one drawn on an ordinary axis, and the price can cross the two on different days.

graphic.title: Same two lows: log-axis line seen on an ordinary axis

items: A trend line carries the slope of past swing points forward.
Different anchors: one line breaks, another holds.
Intraday and closing rules can disagree.
False breaks are labeled only afterward.

lessons.title: Base Rates: Judging a Pattern's Record
lessons.summary: Why a pattern's hit rate means little until it is compared with how often prices rose anyway, and how frequent signals, small samples, and trading costs shrink or erase an apparent edge.

beats.text: A claim that a pattern was followed by a rise 55 percent of the time sounds like evidence, but it is missing a comparison.
Here: how often the price was higher after any comparable period.

terms.definition: How often an outcome happened across all comparable past cases, whether or not a pattern appeared.

graphic.title: Base rate

steps.title: Count those followed by a rise

beats.text: Here: how often the price was higher after periods when the pattern appeared.

terms.definition: How often an outcome happened among only the cases where a given pattern or signal appeared.

graphic.title: Conditional frequency

steps.title: Count those followed by a rise

beats.text: A pattern only carries information if those two numbers differ.
Each dot in this 10 × 10 grid is an illustrative past case. 11 of the 20 ringed pattern cases are filled, meaning the price was higher afterward; so are 44 of the other 80.
Across the 100 cases, that is 11 of 20 (55%) with the pattern and 44 of 80 (55%) without it, so the pattern adds no information here.

graphic.title: Price higher afterward: 55% either way

beats.heading: A rule that fires often
beats.text: With the same 55 percent base rate, a rule signaling on many days with no real information would still see a rise after roughly 55 percent of its signals.

graphic.title: A rule with no real information

steps.title: A rule fires on many days

beats.text: Each of those rises looks like a success. Signals followed by a fall are false positives.

terms.definition: A signal that appeared but was not followed by the outcome it is supposed to point to.

graphic.title: Roughly 55 percent of signals rise anyway

beats.text: Quoting a hit rate without the base rate turns the market's ordinary behavior into an apparent skill.
Over 1,000 past days, the price was higher five days later after 116 of 200 signal days and 472 of the other 800 days.

check.question: What does the comparison show?
choices: 58%: an 8-point edge over a coin flip
Right 116 times, enough to show reliability
check.explanation: The fair comparison is with the days without the signal: 116 of 200 is 58 percent and 472 of 800 is 59 percent. The signal's record is no better than what happened without it.

beats.heading: Small samples
beats.text: Take a coin with an exact 50 percent chance of heads, and flip it 20 times.
The chance of getting 12 or more heads, a record of 60 percent or better, is about 25 percent.
So a rule that fired 20 times and was right 12 times is easy to produce by luck alone.

graphic.title: About 25% of 20-flip runs reach 12 heads

beats.text: Test many rules on the same history and some post records like that by chance: the data-mining problem from lesson 6, in numbers.

graphic.title: Many tests, some lucky records

steps.title: Some post strong records by chance

beats.text: Careful research makes exactly this comparison. The 2000 study by Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky, and Jiang Wang, discussed in lesson 4, is one example.

graphic.title: A base-rate comparison in research

beats.text: It compared the distribution of daily stock returns conditioned on patterns such as head-and-shoulders or double bottoms with the unconditional distribution, a form of base-rate comparison.
It reported that several patterns provided incremental information and may have some practical value.
Testing many ideas raises the bar for believing any one of them.

terms.definition: Trying many rules or factors on the same data, which raises the odds that some look significant by luck.

graphic.title: Multiple testing raises the bar

beats.text: A 2014 NBER working paper by Campbell Harvey, Yan Liu, and Heqing Zhu studied factors proposed to explain differences in expected stock returns; hundreds had been proposed.

terms.definition: An estimate divided by its standard error; a larger value makes a result harder to explain as chance.

graphic.title: The t-ratio

beats.text: They argued that, after hundreds of factors, the usual significance cutoff of a t-ratio above 2.0 does not make sense for a newly discovered factor.
Their model suggests such a factor needs a t-ratio above 3.0.

graphic.title: t-ratio cutoff for a new factor

beats.text: They studied factors rather than chart patterns, but the problem of many tests applies to both.

graphic.title: Factors and chart patterns share the problem

beats.heading: Costs can flip a thin edge
beats.text: Even an edge that is real can be too thin to survive trading costs.

graphic.title: Costs can flip a thin edge

beats.text: As an illustration, suppose a rule is right 55 percent of the time and each trade gains or loses 0.5 percent.
Before costs, the average trade earns 0.55 × 0.5 − 0.45 × 0.5 = 0.05 percent.

graphic.title: Average trade before costs: 0.05 percent

terms.meaning: Percent gained or lost per trade

beats.text: If a round trip costs 0.1 percent in commissions and spread, the average trade loses 0.05 percent.
FINRA notes that frequent trading can come with higher costs that might erode returns, as well as potential tax implications.

graphic.title: Frequent trading, per FINRA

Frequent signals collect base-rate successes and false positives.
Small samples and many tests produce lucky records.
A thin edge can turn negative after costs.

courses.title: Bonds, Rates and the Yield Curve
courses.summary: How a bond's price and yield are linked, why longer bonds swing more, what the yield curve and its inversions show, how real yields and breakeven inflation are read, how the policy rate connects to everyday rates, why company bonds pay a credit spread over Treasuries, and how the Treasury auctions new debt.

lessons.title: Price and Yield
lessons.summary: Face value, coupon and maturity, and why a bond's market price and its yield move in opposite directions.

charts.title: Price of an illustrative 10-year, 4 percent bond at different yields
charts.caption: As the yield required by buyers rises from 1 percent to 8 percent, the price of the same bond falls from well above face value to well below it. The curve bends rather than running straight, so a fall in yields lifts the price by more than an equal rise in yields lowers it.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed points for a 10-year, 4 percent coupon bond, not real market data.

markers.label: Yield equals coupon: price equals face value

beats.heading: A loan you can trade
beats.text: A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable certificate. The borrower, called the issuer, might be a national government, a city, or a company.

graphic.title: A bond is a loan you can trade

steps.title: Issuer borrows money
steps.detail: A government, a city or a company

steps.title: Lender gets a tradable certificate
steps.detail: It can be sold to someone else

beats.text: The lender is whoever holds the bond. Three numbers are printed into the deal at the start.

terms.definition: The fixed amount the issuer repays when the bond matures, commonly $1,000 per bond in the United States.
The fixed interest payment written into the bond, quoted as a yearly percentage of face value and paid on a set schedule.

graphic.title: The coupon, in dollars a year

terms.definition: The date on which the loan ends and the issuer repays the face value to whoever holds the bond.

graphic.title: From issue to maturity

steps.title: Coupons paid on a set schedule

beats.text: Treasury notes and bonds, for example, pay their coupon every six months and repay face value on the maturity date.

terms.definition: The return a buyer earns at the price actually paid, taking into account the coupons and the repayment of face value at maturity.

graphic.title: What goes into a bond's yield

beats.heading: Fixed coupon, moving price
beats.text: The coupon never changes, but the price a bond trades at does. That is the whole puzzle.

graphic.title: What is fixed and what moves

beats.text: Suppose an illustrative bond has a $1,000 face value and a 4 percent coupon, so it pays $40 a year.
If newly issued bonds of the same quality start paying 5 percent, nobody pays $1,000 for the old bond to collect only $40.

graphic.title: At $1,000, the old bond yields less
graphic.note: Old bond: $40 a year on a $1,000 price

beats.text: Its price drops until $40 works out to roughly 5 percent of the purchase price, which is about $800.
The reverse holds too. If new bonds pay only 3 percent, the old bond's $40 looks generous.

graphic.title: Lower going yields push the old bond's price up

beats.text: Buyers bid its price up toward about $1,333, where $40 is roughly 3 percent of the price.

beats.heading: The arithmetic is simplified on purpose
beats.text: The $800 and $1,333 figures use the simplest version of yield: the yearly coupon divided by the price.
A full yield-to-maturity calculation also counts the gain or loss from being repaid exactly $1,000 at maturity, which pulls the price back toward face value as the end date nears.

graphic.title: Price is pulled toward face value near maturity
graphic.note: Drawn with the going yield unchanged along the way

beats.text: The direction is identical in both versions: price and yield move in opposite directions. Push the price up and the yield comes down; let the price fall and the yield rises.
Why? A fixed coupon paid on a higher price works out to a smaller percentage.
Take an illustrative 10-year, 4 percent bond. As the yield required by buyers rises from 1 percent to 8 percent, its price falls from well above face value to well below it.
The curve bends rather than running straight, so a fall in yields lifts the price by more than an equal rise in yields lowers it.
Notice what did not change. The issuer still owes $40 a year and $1,000 at the end. Whoever holds the bond to maturity collects exactly that.

graphic.title: What the issuer still owes

beats.text: Price moves only matter to someone buying or selling before the end date.

beats.heading: Coupon versus going yield
beats.text: TreasuryDirect describes the price of a note or bond as depending on the gap between its coupon rate and the yield buyers demand.

graphic.title: The coupon-yield gap sets the price

beats.text: A coupon equal to the going yield sells at par.

check.question: Bond: fixed $50 coupon, $1,000 face. Comparable new yields fall from 5 to 4 percent. Its price?
check.explanation: The coupon is fixed at $50. When new bonds pay only 4 percent, buyers bid up the old bond until its $50 works out to roughly 4 percent of the price, which is above $1,000.

items: Face value, coupon and maturity are fixed; price moves.
Price and yield move in opposite directions.
Held to maturity: coupons plus face value.
Coupon above going yield means price above par.

lessons.title: Duration and Interest-Rate Risk
lessons.summary: Why a bond with a longer maturity moves more in price for the same change in rates, and how duration puts a number on that sensitivity.

charts.title: Illustrative price change for a one-percentage-point move in yield, by maturity
charts.caption: Three illustrative bonds with the same coupon. A one-point rise in yields barely dents the 2-year bond but knocks roughly 15 percent off the 30-year bond. A one-point fall lifts each by more than the matching rise lowers it.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed values for bonds of equal coupon, not real market data.

beats.heading: How much does price move?
beats.text: A bond's price falls when yields rise. But by how much? The answer depends mostly on how long the money is tied up.

graphic.title: Same yield move, bigger price swing for longer bonds

beats.text: A bond maturing in two years returns its face value soon, so a buyer is stuck with an old coupon for only a short time.

graphic.title: A two-year bond hands money back soon

steps.title: Old coupon held a short time

beats.text: A bond maturing in thirty years locks in that coupon for decades.

left.label: Two-year bond
left.detail: old coupon for a short time

beats.text: Every one of those distant payments is worth less when competing rates rise, and there are many more of them.

graphic.title: A distant payment loses more value when rates rise
graphic.note: The same future payment, valued at two rates one point apart

beats.text: So the price of the long bond has to fall much further to compete.

terms.definition: The risk that a rise in market interest rates lowers the price of an existing bond before it matures.

graphic.title: How interest-rate risk shows up

beats.heading: Duration puts a number on it
beats.text: Duration is the approximate percentage change in a bond's price for a one-percentage-point change in its yield.

graphic.title: Duration as a rule of thumb

beats.text: A bond with a duration of 2 moves roughly 2 percent for each point; a bond with a duration of 15 moves roughly 15 percent.

terms.definition: The unit for a change in a rate itself, so a move from 3 percent to 4 percent is one percentage point.

beats.text: Duration is quoted in years because it is closely tied to the weighted average time until the bond's cash comes back.

graphic.title: Duration sits before the final payment
graphic.note: Duration: the weighted average time until the bond's cash comes back

beats.text: Longer maturity and lower coupon both push duration up, because more of the value sits in the distant future.

terms.definition: A bond that pays no periodic interest and is sold below face value; its duration is close to, and slightly below, its full maturity.

graphic.title: A zero-coupon bond: one payment at maturity
graphic.note: All the value arrives at the end, so duration sits just below maturity

beats.text: Three illustrative bonds share the same coupon. A one-point rise in yields barely dents the 2-year bond but knocks roughly 15 percent off the 30-year bond.
A one-point fall lifts each bond by more than the matching rise lowers it.
Investor.gov's guide to bonds puts it plainly: held to maturity, a bond returns its face value plus interest, but sold before then it may fetch more or less than face value.

graphic.title: Held to maturity or sold before

beats.text: Duration measures the size of that in-between swing. It says nothing about whether the issuer is able to pay, which is a separate risk called credit risk.

graphic.title: Two different risks

beats.text: Duration also explains why the Treasury's longest securities behave so differently from its shortest.
A Treasury bill maturing in a few weeks has almost no duration, so its price hardly moves when rates change.

left.label: Treasury bill
left.detail: matures in weeks; almost no duration

beats.text: A 30-year Treasury bond, described on TreasuryDirect as paying interest every six months for up to three decades, carries a large duration.
It can gain or lose a substantial share of its value in a single year of rate changes, even though the government's promise to pay is identical in both cases.

check.question: Bonds with equal coupons and issuer mature in 3 and 25 years. Yields rise one point. Then:
check.explanation: Duration rises with maturity. The 25-year bond locks in the old coupon for far longer, so its price must fall much further before its yield matches the new market rate.

items: Interest-rate risk: rate moves change a bond's price before maturity.
Duration: rough percent price change per one-point yield move.
Longer maturity and lower coupon raise duration.
Duration says nothing about credit risk.

lessons.title: The Yield Curve
lessons.summary: What you see when you plot yields by maturity, why the line usually slopes upward, and where the public data comes from.

charts.title: Three illustrative yield curves
charts.caption: The normal curve climbs about 1.5 points from the shortest to the longest maturity. The flat curve barely moves. The inverted curve starts high and drifts lower as maturity lengthens. Real curves rarely look this tidy, but these are the three shapes analysts name.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed curves, not real Treasury yields.

beats.heading: A simple picture
beats.text: Take one borrower, usually the U.S. Treasury, and line up its debt from the shortest maturity to the longest: a few weeks, one year, two years, ten years, thirty years.

graphic.title: One borrower's debt, shortest to longest

beats.heading: The yield curve
beats.text: Plot the yield of each on a chart with maturity along the bottom and yield up the side, then connect the dots. The resulting line is the yield curve.

graphic.title: Connect the dots: the yield curve

beats.text: It answers one question at a glance: how much more, or less, does the market demand to lend to the same borrower for a longer stretch of time?

graphic.title: How much more to lend for longer?
graphic.note: When the curve slopes down, longer lending pays less instead

beats.heading: Normal
beats.text: Most of the time the line slopes upward, which is called a normal curve. Two ideas explain the slope.

graphic.title: 10-year minus 3-month spread, yearly average
graphic.note: Above zero, long yields topped short ones. Yearly averages smooth over brief dips

source.organization: FRED (data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
source.title: 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 3-Month Treasury Constant Maturity

beats.text: First, long yields bundle in expectations about where short rates are headed, so if the market expects short rates to climb, long yields sit higher.
Second, lenders usually want extra compensation for locking money away for years, because a long bond carries more interest-rate risk, as the last lesson showed.

graphic.title: Expectations plus a term premium

terms.definition: The extra yield lenders demand for committing money for a longer period and bearing more interest-rate risk.

graphic.title: What a long yield bundles together

beats.heading: Flat and inverted
beats.text: When the two ideas pull in opposite directions the curve can flatten. When expectations of falling short rates overpower the premium it can slope downward, which is called inverted.
Side by side: a normal curve rises from left to right, a flat curve runs level, and an inverted curve slopes downward as longer maturities yield less than shorter ones.
In these illustrative curves, the normal one climbs about 1.5 points from the shortest to the longest maturity. The flat curve barely moves.
The inverted curve starts high and drifts lower as maturity lengthens. Real curves rarely look this tidy, but these are the three shapes analysts name.

check.question: 30-year yields top 3-month yields. What fits the term-premium idea?
choices: Extra yield for longer lending and more rate risk
The central bank sets each maturity
check.explanation: The term premium is compensation for tying money up longer and accepting bigger price swings if rates change. The borrower is the same at every maturity, so repayment odds do not explain the slope.

beats.heading: Where the real curve is published
beats.text: The U.S. Treasury publishes a Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve on its Interest Rate Statistics pages.
Its frequently-asked-questions page explains that the curve is built from closing bid quotes on Treasury securities and read at fixed maturity points.

graphic.title: How Treasury builds its par yield curve

beats.text: So a point on the curve may not match the yield of any single bond. The chart here is a sketch of shapes, not a copy of that data.

terms.definition: The Treasury's published curve, built so that each point is the coupon rate at which a bond of that maturity would trade at face value.

graphic.title: What one point on the par curve means

steps.title: Find the coupon priced at par
That coupon rate is the point

items: Yield curve: one borrower's yields by maturity.
Upward is normal, level is flat, downward is inverted.
Long yields blend expected short rates and a term premium.
Treasury publishes the daily par yield curve.

lessons.title: Inversions and What They Have Signaled
lessons.summary: What it means when short yields sit above long yields, and the documented record linking past inversions to later recessions.

charts.title: An illustrative 10-year minus 3-month spread crossing below zero
charts.caption: The spread narrows month by month, turns negative around month 10, stays inverted for several months, then climbs back above zero. On a real chart, analysts would compare the timing of such a crossing with the later dates of any recession.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — a hand-designed spread path, not real Treasury data.

beats.text: An inverted yield curve is one where short-term yields are higher than long-term yields, so the line slopes downward.

beats.heading: The spread
beats.text: Analysts usually track it with a single number called the spread: a long yield minus a short yield.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, for instance, uses the 10-year Treasury yield minus the 3-month Treasury bill yield.
When that spread is positive the curve is normal. When it falls below zero the curve has inverted.
Inversion is unusual because it means lenders accept less to commit money for ten years than for three months.

check.question: 10-year yield 3.8 percent, 3-month bill 4.3 percent. Which is accurate?
choices: Flat, because the yields are close
check.explanation: The spread is the long yield minus the short yield: 3.8 minus 4.3 equals -0.5 percentage points. A negative spread means short yields exceed long yields, which is the definition of an inverted curve.

beats.heading: Why would that happen?
beats.text: Recall that long yields bundle in expectations about future short rates.

graphic.title: Recall: what a long yield bundles

beats.text: Suppose markets expect the central bank to cut short rates substantially in the years ahead, perhaps because the economy is expected to weaken.

graphic.title: If markets expect the short rate to be cut

beats.text: Then a ten-year yield can settle below the short rate of the moment.
An inversion is therefore often read as the market's collective guess that short rates are on their way down.

graphic.title: An inverted curve can reflect expected cuts
graphic.note: A long yield averages the short rates expected along the way

beats.text: That guess can be right or wrong, and it can be driven by many things besides the outlook for growth.

graphic.title: A guess shaped by many forces

steps.title: Can turn out right or wrong

beats.text: In a 2018 Economic Letter, economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco documented that every U.S. recession in the preceding sixty years had been preceded by a negative term spread.
The same letter documented that a negative spread was followed by a recession in all but one case.
The Cleveland Fed's yield-curve page likewise records that inversions preceded each of the last eight recessions.
It also lists three notable false signals, including the long inversion that ran from late 2022 through late 2024. The pattern is real, and so are the exceptions.

graphic.title: The 2022–2024 inversion, month by month
graphic.note: Monthly averages; below zero, 3-month yields topped 10-year yields

source.organization: FRED (data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
source.title: 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 3-Month Treasury Constant Maturity

beats.text: In this illustrative spread, the gap narrows month by month, turns negative around month 10 and stays inverted for several months, then climbs back above zero.
On a real chart, analysts would compare the timing of such a crossing with the later dates of any recession.

beats.heading: Association is not prediction
beats.text: The record above is a description of the past, not a forecast.

graphic.title: Association is not prediction

beats.text: Inversions have come before recessions with gaps ranging from a few months to about two years, and some inversions were not followed by any recession.

graphic.title: What followed past inversions

beats.text: The economy has changed in ways that could weaken or strengthen the link.
Some Reserve Bank researchers urge caution against reading the signal too literally, while others have found that its record holds up.

graphic.title: Researchers read the signal differently

beats.text: This lesson explains why people watch the spread; it does not say what any inversion means for the future.

graphic.title: What this lesson does and does not do

items: Inversion: short yields exceed long; the spread turns negative.
Often read as markets expecting lower short rates.
Past U.S. recessions were preceded by inversions, with exceptions.
That record is history, not a forecast.

lessons.title: Real vs Nominal
lessons.summary: The difference between a yield on paper and a yield after inflation, and how inflation-protected securities are built.

charts.title: Illustrative nominal yield, inflation, and the real yield left over
charts.caption: Each year shows three bars. Nominal yield and inflation move around, and the real yield is what remains after subtracting one from the other. In years 3 and 4 a higher nominal yield still leaves only a 1 percent real yield because inflation climbed with it.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed yearly values, not real yields or inflation readings.

beats.heading: Nominal yield
beats.text: The yield printed on a bond is a nominal yield: the percentage of money you receive, counted in dollars. It says nothing about what those dollars buy.

graphic.title: Two ways to count a yield

terms.definition: The stated yield counted in money terms, before any adjustment for changes in the general price level.
A sustained rise in the general level of prices, which lowers what each dollar can buy over time.

graphic.title: Rising prices shrink what a dollar buys

beats.text: If a bond yields 5 percent while prices in stores rise 3 percent, the lender's purchasing power grows by only about 2 percent.
That leftover is the real yield. As a rule of thumb:

terms.definition: The nominal yield adjusted for inflation; approximately the nominal yield minus the inflation rate.

graphic.title: Real yield, as a rule of thumb

beats.text: When inflation runs above the nominal yield, the real yield is negative, and the lender ends up able to buy less than before even though the account balance grew.

graphic.title: When inflation tops the yield, real yield turns negative

beats.text: Each year shows three bars. Nominal yield and inflation move around, and the real yield is what remains after subtracting one from the other.
In years 3 and 4 a higher nominal yield still leaves only a 1 percent real yield because inflation climbed with it.

check.question: An illustrative bond has a nominal yield of 4 percent. Over the year, prices rise 5 percent. What is the approximate real yield?
check.explanation: Real yield is roughly nominal yield minus inflation: 4 percent minus 5 percent is about -1 percent. The dollars grew, but they buy slightly less than before.

beats.text: An ordinary bond leaves the lender exposed to this gap, because its coupon and face value are fixed in dollars no matter what prices do.

graphic.title: A 4% yield when prices rise 5% a year
graphic.note: Buying power: the balance measured in starting prices

beats.text: The U.S. Treasury also issues a security designed to remove that exposure: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, sold with maturities of 5, 10 and 30 years.

terms.definition: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, whose principal is adjusted with a consumer price index so the return is set in real terms.

graphic.title: What TIPS change

beats.text: Their principal is adjusted up or down in line with a consumer price index.
The coupon rate is fixed, but because it is applied to the adjusted principal, the dollar amount of each interest payment rises when prices rise and falls when they fall.

graphic.title: Fixed rate, moving interest payment

beats.heading: How the adjustment works, in numbers
beats.text: Take an illustrative TIPS with $1,000 of original principal and a 1 percent coupon.
If the price index rises 3 percent over a year, the principal is adjusted to about $1,030 and the yearly interest becomes about $10.30 instead of $10.00.

graphic.title: A 3% index rise, in dollars

beats.text: At maturity, TreasuryDirect states that the holder receives the adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is greater.

graphic.title: At maturity: the greater of the two principals

beats.text: So a period of falling prices cannot push the final repayment below the starting $1,000.
Because a TIPS coupon is quoted in real terms, its yield can be compared with the nominal yield on an ordinary Treasury of the same maturity.

beats.heading: Breakeven inflation rate
beats.text: The gap between the two is sometimes called the breakeven inflation rate: roughly the average inflation at which the two securities would deliver the same result.
The Treasury publishes a separate Daily Treasury Par Real Yield Curve alongside its nominal curve so that both can be read from the same source.

graphic.title: Two curves from the same source

items: Nominal yield counts dollars; real yield counts what they buy.
Real yield ≈ nominal minus inflation; it can be negative.
TIPS principal moves with a price index.
TIPS repay at least the original principal.

lessons.title: The Policy Rate and the Curve
lessons.summary: How the Federal Reserve sets a target for the shortest rate, why long rates do not simply follow it, and how the two reach mortgages and savings accounts.

charts.title: An illustrative policy rate and 10-year yield over twenty quarters
charts.caption: The short rate climbs in steps from 0.5 percent to 4.5 percent and then comes back down. The long rate drifts up by far less and then eases. Where the short rate rises above the long rate, around quarters 10 to 16, the illustrative curve is inverted.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed paths for a policy rate and a long yield, not real data.

beats.text: The very short end of the yield curve is anchored by the central bank.

graphic.title: The central bank anchors the short end

beats.text: In the United States the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, meets eight times a year on a published schedule and sets the policy rate target.

terms.definition: The interest rate at which banks lend reserve balances to one another overnight; the FOMC sets a target range for it.

graphic.title: A target range for the overnight rate

beats.text: The Federal Reserve then uses its policy tools, including the interest it pays on bank reserves and its open market purchases and sales of securities, to keep the overnight rate inside that range.

graphic.title: Tools that hold the rate in range

steps.title: Policy tools
steps.detail: Interest on reserves, open market operations

steps.title: Overnight rate kept in the range

beats.heading: The policy rate
beats.text: Because this rate is set by decision rather than by supply and demand alone, it is called the policy rate.
Longer rates are not set by the committee.

graphic.title: Who sets which rate

beats.text: A ten-year yield reflects what the market expects the policy rate to average over the next ten years, plus the term premium.
So when the FOMC raises its target, the two-year yield usually follows closely.

right.label: Ten-year yield
right.detail: may rise less, stay put, or fall

beats.text: But the ten-year yield may rise less, stay put, or even fall if investors conclude the increase makes future cuts more likely.
This is why the curve flattens or inverts during many tightening cycles and steepens when the policy rate is cut.

graphic.title: Policy rate and 10-year yield, 2021–2025
graphic.note: Monthly averages; the funds rate sat above the 10-year from Dec 2022 to Dec 2024

source.organization: FRED (data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System)
source.title: Federal Funds Effective Rate; Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis

beats.text: The central bank moves one end of the seesaw; the other end moves according to expectations.

graphic.title: Two ends, moved by different forces

beats.text: In an illustrative path over twenty quarters, the short rate climbs in steps from 0.5 percent to 4.5 percent and then comes back down.
The long rate drifts up by far less and then eases. Where the short rate rises above the long rate, around quarters 10 to 16, the illustrative curve is inverted.
The policy rate matters to households because other rates are priced off the curve.

graphic.title: From the policy rate to households

steps.title: Policy rate anchors the short end
Other rates priced off the curve
Households borrow and save at them

beats.text: Savings accounts, money market funds and short certificates of deposit tend to track the short end, so their rates move soon after the FOMC acts.

graphic.title: The short end responds quickly

steps.title: Savings and CD rates follow soon

beats.text: A 30-year fixed mortgage is priced closer to long Treasury yields, which is why mortgage rates can move before a policy meeting, on expectations, and sometimes barely react to the meeting itself.

graphic.title: Priced off different ends of the curve

check.question: The FOMC raises its target range a quarter point. What fits?
choices: Short yields rise; 10-year may rise less, hold, or fall
check.explanation: The committee anchors only the shortest rate. Longer yields reflect expected future policy plus a term premium, so they need not move in step, and they can move ahead of a meeting on expectations.

terms.definition: The chain by which a change in the policy rate reaches borrowing and saving rates across the economy.

beats.text: The Federal Reserve describes this chain as the transmission of monetary policy, and those effects build over time.

beats.heading: Two ends, two stories
beats.text: A useful habit is to ask which end of the curve a rate belongs to.

graphic.title: Which end does a rate belong to?

beats.text: Credit cards and savings rates live near the short end and follow the policy rate closely.

graphic.title: Near the short end: follows the policy rate

beats.text: Long mortgages and long-term borrowing costs live near the long end and follow expectations and the term premium.

graphic.title: Near the long end: follows expectations

beats.text: Both are shaped by the central bank, but only one is set by it.

items: The FOMC target anchors the short end.
Long yields reflect expected short rates plus a term premium.
Savings track the short end; long mortgages track long yields.
Transmission effects take time to build.

lessons.title: Credit Spreads
lessons.summary: Why a company's bond yields more than a Treasury of similar maturity, how credit ratings sort bonds into investment grade and high yield, and how spreads widened in a documented stress episode.

charts.title: Illustrative 10-year yields for the Treasury and two companies through a stress episode
charts.caption: In months 1 to 9 the higher-rated company yields 1.2 points more than the Treasury and the lower-rated company 3.5 points more. As stress hits, the Treasury yield dips from 3.9 percent in month 9 to 3.4 percent in month 11, yet the lower-rated company's yield climbs from 7.4 to 10.4 percent, as its spread doubles to 7.0 points. The higher-rated spread peaks at 2.4 points in the same month. By month 24 both spreads are back at their starting levels.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed yields for a Treasury and two unnamed companies, not real market data.

beats.heading: The ruler
beats.text: Treasury yields are the ruler other borrowers are measured against.

graphic.title: Treasury yields: the ruler for other borrowers

beats.text: A company that sells a 10-year bond has to offer more than a 10-year Treasury pays, because lending to a company brings risks beyond those of the Treasury benchmark.

graphic.title: Same maturity, different borrower

terms.definition: The extra yield, in percentage points, that a bond pays over a Treasury security of similar maturity.

beats.text: So a corporate bond's yield can be read as two stacked pieces: the Treasury yield for a similar maturity, plus a spread for what is different about this borrower and this bond.

Picture three bars: Treasury, a higher-rated company and a lower-rated company. All share the same Treasury yield at the bottom; each company bar adds a credit spread, taller for the lower-rated company.
The Federal Reserve Board's 2020 annual report tracks spreads in this form, as corporate bond yields over comparable-maturity Treasury yields.

graphic.title: How the Board's report measures spreads

beats.text: One piece of the spread pays for default risk.

terms.definition: The risk that a borrower fails to make timely payments of interest or principal on its bonds.

graphic.title: What default means for a bondholder

steps.title: Spread partly pays for this risk

beats.text: An SEC investor bulletin on corporate bonds names this as one key risk to bondholders. Credit rating agencies assign ratings based on their evaluation of that risk and may revise them.

graphic.title: How a credit rating works

beats.text: A later SEC bulletin on credit ratings explains that some agencies split their scales between the BBB and BB categories.

terms.definition: A non-investment-grade bond, also called speculative, which generally pays a higher interest rate to compensate for greater risk.

graphic.title: Two sides of the rating split
graphic.note: On scales that split between BBB and BB

beats.text: Those lower-rated bonds generally offer higher interest rates to compensate for greater risk, so the spread segment generally grows as the rating falls.

check.question: 10-year yields: Treasury 4.0, A-rated 5.1, BB-rated 7.2 percent. Investment grade splits at BBB/BB. Which is true?
check.explanation: Spread is yield minus the Treasury yield: 7.2 minus 4.0 is 3.2 points; 5.1 minus 4.0 is 1.1 for the A bond. BB sits below BBB-, so it is non-investment grade, or high yield.

beats.text: Default risk is not the whole story. The credit ratings bulletin notes that a rating does not reflect market or liquidity risk, and that even debt rated at the top of the scale sometimes defaults.

graphic.title: What a credit rating reflects
graphic.note: Even top-rated debt sometimes defaults

terms.definition: The ability to sell a bond for cash when the owner chooses; bonds that trade often and in high volumes may be more liquid.

graphic.title: More and less liquid bonds

beats.text: The corporate bond bulletin describes liquidity risk as the chance that a seller may not receive a price that reflects the bond's true value.

graphic.title: Liquidity risk

beats.text: Bond terms matter too: some bonds let the company buy them back before maturity, which the corporate bond bulletin calls call risk.

graphic.title: Call risk

steps.title: Terms let the company buy back

beats.text: In an illustrative calm stretch, months 1 to 9, the higher-rated company yields 1.2 points more than the Treasury and the lower-rated company 3.5 points more.
As stress hits, the Treasury yield dips from 3.9 percent in month 9 to 3.4 percent in month 11.
Yet the lower-rated company's yield climbs from 7.4 to 10.4 percent, as its spread doubles to 7.0 points. The higher-rated spread peaks at 2.4 points in the same month.
By month 24 both spreads are back at their starting levels.

beats.heading: A documented stress episode
beats.text: Federal Reserve records show this pattern in early 2020. The Board's 2020 annual report states that corporate bond spreads over comparable-maturity Treasury yields increased significantly early in the pandemic.

graphic.title: What the Board's 2020 report records

beats.text: That was a period when liquidity conditions in that market had deteriorated.
A Board FEDS Notes article of October 7, 2020, describes spreads widening dramatically while new issuance halted.
Spreads then eased substantially in the days after the Federal Reserve and the Treasury announced a corporate bond buying facility on March 23, 2020, before it had bought a single bond.

graphic.title: Early 2020: widening, then a facility
graphic.note: Spreads eased before the facility had bought a single bond

beats.text: The chart in this lesson is a sketch of that kind of pattern, not the data.

items: Corporate yield = Treasury yield plus a credit spread.
On such scales, BBB- or higher is investment grade.
High-yield bonds pay more for greater risk.
Ratings do not cover liquidity or call risk.

lessons.title: Breakeven Inflation and the Real Yield Curve
lessons.summary: How the breakeven inflation rate is computed from nominal and inflation-protected Treasury yields, what it contains besides expected inflation, and how to read a real yield below zero.

charts.title: An illustrative nominal yield, real yield and the breakeven between them
charts.caption: The breakeven line is the nominal yield minus the real yield. From month 5 to month 18 the real yield is below zero while the nominal yield stays positive, so the breakeven sits above the nominal yield. In month 8 the nominal yield is 1.0 percent and the real yield is −1.0 percent, a breakeven of 2.0 points.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — hand-designed yields for a 10-year nominal note and a 10-year TIPS, not real Treasury data.

beats.text: Put a nominal Treasury note and a TIPS of about the same maturity side by side.
The nominal yield is stated in dollars, so it has to cover inflation; the TIPS yield is stated in real terms, because inflation is paid through the principal adjustment.

graphic.title: Where inflation shows up

beats.heading: Breakeven inflation rate
beats.text: Nominal yield minus TIPS yield is the breakeven inflation rate. The gap between the taller nominal bar and the shorter TIPS real yield bar shows it.
Federal Reserve Board economists note that this spread, also called inflation compensation, has often been used as a real-time proxy for market participants' inflation expectations.
An illustrative 10-year Treasury note yields 4.30 percent and a 10-year TIPS yields 1.90 percent, so the breakeven is 4.30 minus 1.90, or 2.40 percentage points.

graphic.title: Nominal minus TIPS yield: the breakeven

beats.text: FRED, the data service of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, publishes a daily 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate.

graphic.title: 10-year breakeven inflation rate, yearly average
graphic.note: 10-year nominal yield minus 10-year TIPS yield, averaged by year

source.organization: FRED (data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
source.title: 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate

beats.text: It is derived from 10-year nominal and inflation-indexed constant maturity Treasury yields, in percent and not seasonally adjusted.

graphic.title: How FRED's breakeven series is built

beats.text: FRED describes it as the inflation market participants expect over the next 10 years, on average.
That shorthand has limits. In the Board note's model, inflation compensation equals expected inflation, plus an inflation risk premium, minus a TIPS liquidity premium.

terms.definition: Extra compensation nominal bond investors demand for bearing inflation risk.

graphic.title: Inflation compensation in the Board note's model

beats.text: The note says it is believed to have been positive and sizable in the 1970s and 1980s and appears to have declined to lower or even negative levels in later decades.

graphic.title: The inflation risk premium over the decades
graphic.note: Shape only; no estimates are plotted

terms.definition: Extra yield on TIPS that mainly reflects their lower liquidity compared with nominal Treasury securities.

graphic.title: Why TIPS carry a liquidity premium

beats.text: It typically lifts TIPS yields above true real yields, pulling the measured breakeven down.
So a breakeven can sit above or below expected inflation, depending on which premium is larger.

graphic.title: Which premium is larger decides the gap
graphic.note: Breakeven sits above expected inflation if the risk premium is larger, below if not

beats.text: In this illustrative chart, the breakeven line is the nominal yield minus the real yield.
The Treasury publishes it next to its nominal par yield curve.

terms.definition: The Treasury's daily curve relating the par real yield on TIPS to time to maturity.

graphic.title: Par real yield curve, beside the nominal one

beats.text: Subtracting the real curve from the nominal curve at the same maturity gives a breakeven for each maturity.
A real yield can also fall below zero. TreasuryDirect states that TIPS auction rules allow negative real yield bids.

graphic.title: 10-year TIPS real yield, yearly average
graphic.note: Below zero on a yearly average in 2012, 2020 and 2021

source.organization: FRED (data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System)
source.title: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis, Inflation-Indexed

beats.text: Under a rule Treasury amended in April 2011, a note or bond auction that produces a yield below 0.125 percent gets a 0.125 percent interest rate, with the price adjusted to a premium.

graphic.title: Treasury's 0.125 percent floor rule
graphic.note: Rule amended in April 2011

beats.text: The small coupon is still paid; paying more than par is what pulls the real yield below zero.

graphic.title: Paying above par pulls the yield below zero

beats.text: When the real yield is negative and the nominal yield is positive, the breakeven exceeds the nominal yield. In the chart, that holds from month 5 to month 18.
In month 8 the nominal yield is 1.0 percent and the real yield is −1.0 percent, a breakeven of 2.0 points.

check.question: 10-year note 3.1 percent, 10-year TIPS −0.4 percent. Which is true?
choices: 3.5-point breakeven mixing expected inflation and premiums
No breakeven; real yields can't be negative
check.explanation: Breakeven is nominal minus real: 3.1 minus −0.4 equals 3.5 points. Fed research splits that spread into expected inflation, an inflation risk premium and a TIPS liquidity premium, and TIPS auctions allow negative real yields.

items: Breakeven: nominal yield minus TIPS real yield.
It also contains two premiums, not just expected inflation.
Nominal curve minus real curve gives each maturity's breakeven.
Negative real yield, positive nominal: breakeven exceeds nominal.

lessons.title: Treasury Auctions
lessons.summary: How the Treasury sells new bills, notes and bonds: the announcement, competitive and noncompetitive bids, the single-price award, and how to read an auction results release.

charts.title: An illustrative $30 billion auction: competitive bids and awards by yield
charts.caption: The offering is $30 billion, and $1.5 billion of noncompetitive bids are accepted first, leaving $28.5 billion for competitive bidders. Bids from 4.20 to 4.25 percent total $27.0 billion and are filled in full. The last $1.5 billion comes from the $5.0 billion bid at 4.26 percent, so those bids receive 30 percent of what they asked for and 4.26 percent is the high yield. Every bid above it is rejected. Total bids of $75.0 billion, including noncompetitive bids, against $30.0 billion accepted give a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.50.
charts.dataNote: Synthetic illustration — a hand-designed set of bids for an unnamed security, not a real Treasury auction.

markers.label: High yield: bids here filled 30 percent

beats.text: The Treasury sells new marketable securities by auction. TreasuryDirect lays out four steps.
Each announcement names the security, the amount offered, the auction, issue and maturity dates, the terms of the offering, and the closing times for bids.

graphic.title: Dates named in an auction announcement
graphic.note: Also named: the security, amount, terms and bid closing times

beats.text: The auction date and the issue date are often a few days or even a few weeks apart.

graphic.title: Auction first, issue later

steps.title: A few days or even weeks

beats.heading: Noncompetitive bids
beats.text: A noncompetitive bid names only an amount, up to $10 million per auction, and accepts whatever rate or yield the auction produces.
Bids through a TreasuryDirect account must be noncompetitive.

beats.heading: Competitive bids
beats.text: A competitive bid names the rate, yield or discount margin the bidder will accept, and must go through a bank, broker or dealer.

graphic.title: Two ways to bid

beats.text: A competitive bid has a maximum of 35 percent of the offering amount. Treasury's auction rules bar a bidder from bidding both ways in the same auction.
The Treasury first accepts all noncompetitive bids that comply with the rules, then accepts competitive bids from the lowest rate or yield upward until the offering is fully awarded.

graphic.title: The order of acceptance

beats.heading: The high yield
beats.text: The highest accepted yield is reported as the high yield, and a 2005 Federal Reserve Bank of New York study calls it the stop.

graphic.title: The high yield, or stop

beats.text: Bids below it are filled in full, bids above it are rejected, and bids at it are prorated.

Every successful bidder, competitive or noncompetitive, receives the same rate or yield as the highest accepted bid and pays the same price, which is why Treasury's rules call this a single-price auction.

graphic.title: One yield, one price for every winner

beats.text: Take an illustrative $30 billion offering. $1.5 billion of noncompetitive bids are accepted first, leaving $28.5 billion for competitive bidders.
Bids from 4.20 to 4.25 percent total $27.0 billion and are filled in full. The last $1.5 billion comes from the $5.0 billion bid at 4.26 percent.

graphic.title: How the $30 billion offering is filled

beats.text: So those bids at 4.26 percent receive 30 percent of what they asked for, and 4.26 percent is the high yield. Every bid above it is rejected.

terms.definition: The total amount of bids tendered divided by the amount accepted, reported in Treasury auction results releases.

beats.text: Total bids of $75.0 billion, including noncompetitive bids, against $30.0 billion accepted give a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.50.

graphic.title: Bid-to-cover: $75.0 billion ÷ $30.0 billion

check.question: High yield 4.26 percent. Bids: competitive at 4.22; noncompetitive for $5,000. Which is accurate?
check.explanation: Every successful bidder gets the high yield and pays one price. Noncompetitive bids are accepted first; only bids exactly at the high yield can be filled in part, so the 4.22 bid fills fully.

beats.heading: Reading a real results release
beats.text: The results press release for a 10-year note auctioned on May 6, 2025, shows each piece.

graphic.title: Announcement versus results release

beats.text: The high yield was 4.342 percent, bids at that yield were allotted 92.86 percent, and all bids at lower yields were accepted in full.

graphic.title: Bids at the 4.342% high yield: 92.86% allotted

proportion.unitLabel: percent of bids at the high yield

beats.text: The interest rate was set at 4-1/4 percent, below the high yield, so the price was 99.260100 per $100 of face value.

graphic.title: Rate below the high yield, price below par

beats.text: A footnote computes the bid-to-cover ratio as $109,378,157,100 tendered divided by $42,000,007,100 accepted, or 2.60, counting both competitive and noncompetitive bids.

graphic.title: Bid-to-cover: tendered ÷ accepted = 2.60

beats.heading: Trading starts before the auction
beats.text: The New York Fed study describes dealers and other market participants trading a new security on a when-issued basis right after its auction is announced.

graphic.title: When-issued trading starts early

terms.definition: Trading in a newly announced Treasury security before it is issued, with settlement on the issue date.

graphic.title: The when-issued window
graphic.note: Trades settle on the issue date

beats.text: It cites a joint report by the Treasury, the SEC and the Federal Reserve Board finding that when-issued trading serves as a price discovery mechanism, giving potential bidders a gauge of demand.

graphic.title: Price discovery before the auction

steps.title: Bidders get a gauge of demand

beats.text: Treasury's auction rules bar anyone holding a when-issued, futures or forward position in the security being auctioned from bidding noncompetitively.

items: Noncompetitive bids up to $10 million go first.
Competitive bids fill from the lowest yield up.
Everyone gets the high yield and one price.
Releases report high yield, allotment and bid-to-cover.
